Learning the closest Slater determinant

Nisarga Paul Email: npaul@caltech.edu Affiliation: Department of Physics and Institute for Quantum Information and Matter, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA    Haimeng Zhao Email: haimeng@caltech.edu Affiliation: Department of Physics and Institute for Quantum Information and Matter, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA    David D. Dai Email: dddai@mit.edu Affiliation: Department of Physics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02139, USA Affiliation: The NSF AI Institute for Artificial Intelligence and Fundamental Interactions
Abstract

Learning compact, interpretable descriptions of quantum many-body states is an important task in quantum science. We study the task of learning the Slater determinant with maximum fidelity to an arbitrary fermionic many-body state, with motivation from both Hartree-Fock methods and agnostic tomography. Given an nn-fermion wavefunction built from mm fermionic modes, we provide classical and quantum algorithms returning a Slater determinant with fidelity within ε\varepsilon of maximal in time mpoly​(n,1/ε)m^{\text{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon)}. We prove matching hardness lower bounds, assuming standard complexity conjectures, along some parameter axes. Given access to quantum copies, we prove this can be accomplished with poly​(m,n,1/ε)\text{poly}(m,n,1/\varepsilon) copies of ρ\rho. We also show that above a fidelity of 2/32/3 any stationary point is the unique global maximum while below 2/32/3 the optimization landscape can have spurious stationary points, and hence 2/32/3 marks a transition point in the optimization landscape for this problem. We apply the algorithm to the Fermi–Hubbard model, extracting the closest Slater determinant from neural quantum state solutions. Together, our results provide algorithmic tools with provable guarantees in understanding fermionic many-body systems with classical or quantum simulation.

I Introduction

Extracting compact, interpretable descriptions of complex many-body wavefunctions is one of the central challenges of quantum science. For fermionic systems, the simplest such description is a Slater determinant, the antisymmetrized product of single-particle states [54]. Despite their simplicity, Slater determinants can capture a remarkable range of quantum many-body phenomena, from molecules and nuclei to ferromagnets and topological phases [13, 28]. Slater determinants form the variational foundation of Hartree-Fock theory and density functional theory—two algorithmic workhorses in condensed matter physics and quantum chemistry—and are the reference around which beyond-mean-field methods such as coupled-cluster [41, 22, 37, 52] expand.

A natural question is then the following: given a fermionic many-body wavefunction, how does one find the closest Slater determinant? We will quantify closeness by having a high fidelity. Despite its apparent simplicity, this question is surprisingly subtle and lacks a complete answer, since the manifold of Slater determinants is nonlinear and it is an essentially non-convex optimization problem (Fig. 1). Prior attempts have involved, for instance, heuristic numerical gradient ascent [75, 74], whose performance is not guaranteed; here, we seek algorithms that provably solve the problem with rigorous performance guarantees.

A precise formulation of this problem is as follows. Let ℋn=∧nℋ1\mathcal{H}_{n}=\wedge^{n}\mathcal{H}_{1} be the Hilbert space of nn-particle fermionic wavefunctions built from single-particle Hilbert space ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}, with dimension m=dimℋ1m=\dim\mathcal{H}_{1} and n≤mn\leq m, and let

𝒮={⋀i=1n|φi⟩:|φi⟩∈ℋ1,⟨φi|φj⟩=δi​j}\mathcal{S}=\left\{\bigwedge_{i=1}^{n}|\varphi_{i}\rangle:|\varphi_{i}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{1},\langle\varphi_{i}|\varphi_{j}\rangle=\delta_{ij}\right\} (1)

be the set of Slater determinants. Given a state in ℋn\mathcal{H}_{n} with density matrix ρ\rho and an error tolerance ε>0\varepsilon>0, we seek |S⟩∈𝒮|S\rangle\in\mathcal{S} such that

⟨S|ρ|S⟩≥𝖮𝖯𝖳−ε,where ​𝖮𝖯𝖳=max|S⟩∈𝒮⁡⟨S|ρ|S⟩.\langle S|\rho|S\rangle\geq\mathsf{OPT}-\varepsilon,\quad\text{where }\mathsf{OPT}=\max_{|S\rangle\in\mathcal{S}}\langle S|\rho|S\rangle. (2)

Here, ρ\rho can be given to us either as a classical description, for applications in analyzing tensor networks or neural quantum states, or as copies of a quantum state produced by a quantum device or quantum simulator. We will be interested in the complexity of a classical or quantum algorithm solving this problem.

This task is fundamental in physical sciences, where we advance our understanding of the physical world by learning simple ansätze to describe complicated quantum states, with the approximation accuracy in mind. This is also of practical interest in both condensed matter physics and quantum technology. On the condensed matter side, this problem is related to (but distinct from) the Hartree-Fock (HF) approximation, which minimizes the energy expectation value of a Hamiltonian HH over 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Here we are maximizing fidelity with a given state ρ\rho, with no reference to a Hamiltonian. In general, the two problems need not coincide unless ρ\rho is the ground state of HH and ρ∈𝒮\rho\in\mathcal{S}. For a numerical practitioner with some compact description of a fermionic state, such as a matrix product state or neural quantum state [72, 51, 14], finding the best Slater determinant approximation allows the extraction of meaningful information such as a natural single-particle occupation basis and notion of particle-hole excitations [39, 49, 60, 52]. On the quantum technology side, algorithms solving this problem can be used to benchmark and understand the outcomes of fermionic quantum simulators and computers, which fall into the broader task of agnostic tomography [32, 17, 78, 69], where the goal is to find a state in some class 𝒞\mathcal{C} maximizing overlap with ρ\rho, without the assurance that ρ∈𝒞\rho\in\mathcal{C}. In particular, our problem is the natural fermionic analog of closest product state learning [17, 8, 71, 66], but the antisymmetry of fermionic wavefunctions renders it structurally quite different. Finally, for an experimentalist with access to copies of ρ\rho, a practical solution to this problem yields a useful proxy for an unknown, potentially complex many-body state.

Results. Our main results are twofold:

  • •

    Learning algorithms. We give a classical and a quantum algorithm to find the closest Slater determinant both with runtime mpoly⁡(n,1/ε)m^{\mathrm{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon)}, polynomial in mm for constant nn and ε\varepsilon. The quantum algorithm has a poly⁡(m,n,1/ε)\mathrm{poly}(m,n,1/\varepsilon) sample complexity. The algorithms truncate ρ\rho to a subspace of “natural orbitals” and perform a discretized search over the corresponding subspace of Slater determinants. Under a standard complexity conjecture, no classical algorithm can substantially improve the runtime dependence in nn. Moreover, no classical or quantum algorithm that runs in time polynomial in 1/ε1/\varepsilon can solve the problem unless 𝖭𝖯⊆𝖡𝖯𝖯/𝖡𝖰𝖯\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{BPP}/\mathsf{BQP}.

  • •

    Optimization landscape. We reveal a sharp, qualitative transition in the optimization landscape of finding the closest Slater determinant. In particular, we show that if a Slater determinant |S⟩|S\rangle is a stationary point of the fidelity and has fidelity F=⟨S|ρ|S⟩>2/3\mathrm{F}=\langle S|\rho|S\rangle>2/3, then it is the global unique closest Slater determinant. In other words, above the threshold of 2/32/3, the fidelity optimization landscape is benign in the sense of lacking spurious stationary points, a strong guarantee in a non-convex optimization problem. Below F=2/3\mathrm{F}=2/3, this guarantee can always be thwarted, and hence 2/32/3 marks a sharp transition in the nature of the optimization landscape (Fig. 1b).

We now describe these results in more detail. We separate the case of classical access to ρ\rho, for which we assume an efficient way to compute amplitudes, and quantum access to ρ\rho, in which case we assume we can make measurements on quantum copies of ρ\rho. In either case, the algorithms proceed by estimating the single-particle reduced density matrix (1-RDM) and isolating a poly⁡(n,1/ε)\mathrm{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon)-dimensional subspace of ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} comprising high-occupancy orbitals. We then discretize the space of Slater determinants comprising these orbitals and find the one with maximum fidelity. This procedure takes mpoly⁡(n,1/ε)m^{\mathrm{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon)} time and, using quantum threshold search [6], consumes a polynomial number of samples in the quantum case. We prove that this time complexity is essentially optimal in 1/ε1/\varepsilon for both the quantum and classical algorithms, and essentially optimal in nn for the classical algorithm, under widely-believed complexity-theoretic assumptions. To establish the latter, we prove that an mo⁡(n)m^{o(n)}-time classical algorithm could also solve the nn-Multicolored Clique problem in an unacceptably small time [20]. For the former, we prove that a poly⁡(m,1/ε)\mathrm{poly}(m,1/\varepsilon)-time algorithm in either the classical or quantum setting would efficiently solve the 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-hard quantum separability problem [26]. We summarize the state of affairs in Table 1.

Our second main result shows that the geometry of the optimization landscape exhibits a sharp, qualitative transition at fidelity 2/32/3. In particular, in Section V we show that spurious stationary points (e.g. local optima) of the fidelity function are forbidden above F=2/3\mathrm{F}=2/3. Moreover, this threshold is sharp in the sense that there exist pure states |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle whose fidelity has stationary points with fidelity arbitrarily close to 2/32/3 from below. The definition of stationarity is provided in Section V, which closely resembles the Brillouin condition from Hartree-Fock theory [12]. Any Slater determinant |S⟩|S\rangle satisfying this condition and F>2/3\mathrm{F}>2/3 is hence guaranteed to be the global optimum, though there may be other stationary points with F<2/3\mathrm{F}<2/3. This is a useful guarantee for an optimization problem otherwise only amenable to a brute-force solution: a heuristic algorithm such as gradient ascent or Hartree-Fock-style iteration, once it reaches a fidelity above 2/32/3, should converge to the global optimum.

We complement these results with numerical experiments, described in Sec. VI. We apply our classical algorithm to ground states of the Fermi–Hubbard model, extracting the closest Slater determinant directly from exact diagonalization (Fig. 1c) or a neural quantum state representation (Fig. 4a). Using 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT} as the ground truth, we find that simple gradient ascent can be unreliable as system grows, and we illustrate the distribution of stationary points within the optimization landscape (Fig. 4b,c).

Related Work. The problem of finding the closest Slater determinant to a given state has been studied empirically using gradient ascent algorithms [3, 75, 74]. These, however, hold no guarantees of convergence to the global optimum, which is our focus. Refs. [1, 45] give poly⁡(n,m,1/ε)\mathrm{poly}(n,m,1/\varepsilon)-efficient solutions to this problem when ρ\rho is known to be a Slater determinant, i.e. 𝖮𝖯𝖳=1\mathsf{OPT}=1. In this setting, the state is entirely specified by its 1-RDM, which can be estimated efficiently [36, 76, 11, 18]. However, this approach does not work here because the 1-RDM by itself does not determine the closest Slater determinant in general11 1 Consider c1†​c2†+c3†​c4†2​|0⟩\frac{c_{1}^{\dagger}c_{2}^{\dagger}+c_{3}^{\dagger}c_{4}^{\dagger}}{\sqrt{2}}|0\rangle and c1†​c3†+c2†​c4†2​|0⟩\frac{c_{1}^{\dagger}c_{3}^{\dagger}+c_{2}^{\dagger}c_{4}^{\dagger}}{\sqrt{2}}|0\rangle, which have identical 1-RDMs ∝I\propto I but different closest Slaters, namely the pairs {c1†​c2†​|0⟩,c3†​c4†​|0⟩}\{c_{1}^{\dagger}c_{2}^{\dagger}|0\rangle,c_{3}^{\dagger}c_{4}^{\dagger}|0\rangle\} and {c1†​c3†​|0⟩,c2†​c4†​|0⟩}\{c_{1}^{\dagger}c_{3}^{\dagger}|0\rangle,c_{2}^{\dagger}c_{4}^{\dagger}|0\rangle\}, respectively.. Indeed, hardness results on learning even free fermion states from measurements [10, 11] serve as precautions for this agnostic tomography problem. We note that several works have proposed using quantities like 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT} to capture the amount of correlations in a fermionic state [30, 31, 9, 63]. Indeed, there is a significant body of literature on correlation measures of fermionic states using non-Gaussianity, non-stabilizerness, occupation number entropies, and more [34, 21, 42, 19, 4, 53, 38, 27, 65, 58].

The closest analog of our problem in the bosonic setting is the problem of learning the closest product state to a given nn-qubit state, recently studied by Bakshi et al. in the setting of quantum copy access [8]. Bakshi et al. give an algorithm with sample and time complexity npoly⁡(1/ε)n^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)} to achieve this task within additive error ε\varepsilon, and also prove computational hardness when the desired accuracy is inverse-polynomial in nn. A product state is specified by independent local factors |π1⟩⊗⋯⊗|πn⟩|\pi_{1}\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|\pi_{n}\rangle, and the algorithm of Bakshi et al. exploits this structure with an algorithm proceeding qubit by qubit. This algorithm does not transfer directly here, since Slaters do not factorize over particles.

Outline. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we present the classical algorithm for learning the closest Slater determinant. In Section III, we give a quantum protocol for the problem. In Section IV, we present computational hardness lower bounds in both the classical and quantum settings. We study the properties of the optimization landscape in Section V, report numerical results in Section VI, and conclude in Section VII.

II Algorithms for learning the closest Slater

We first establish some notation. We take ℋn=∧nℋ1\mathcal{H}_{n}=\wedge^{n}\mathcal{H}_{1} to be the Hilbert space of nn-particle fermionic wavefunctions where ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} is the single-particle Hilbert space. We set m=dimℋ1m=\dim\mathcal{H}_{1} and n≤mn\leq m. Then

𝒮={⋀i=1n|φi⟩:|φi⟩∈ℋ1,⟨φi|φj⟩=δi​j}\mathcal{S}=\left\{\bigwedge_{i=1}^{n}|\varphi_{i}\rangle:|\varphi_{i}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{1},\langle\varphi_{i}|\varphi_{j}\rangle=\delta_{ij}\right\} (3)

is the set of Slater determinants (or Slaters for short). We denote Slaters by capital letters, e.g., |S⟩|S\rangle, |T⟩|T\rangle. Let ρ\rho be an arbitrary fermionic state, either pure or mixed. When ρ\rho is pure, we write ρ=|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|\rho=|\psi\rangle\!\langle\psi| where |ψ⟩∈ℋn|\psi\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{n}. We center the main text around pure states to lighten exposition, generalizing to the mixed state case in Appendix B. We will optimize the fidelity,

F​(S)=⟨S|ρ|S⟩,\text{F}(S)=\langle S|\rho|S\rangle, (4)

where we assume unit normalization Tr⁡ρ=⟨S|S⟩=1\Tr\rho=\langle S|S\rangle=1.

Let |0⟩|0\rangle be the zero particle vacuum. Let c1†,…,cm†c_{1}^{\dagger},\ldots,c_{m}^{\dagger} create an orthonormal basis |φ1⟩,…,|φm⟩|\varphi_{1}\rangle,\ldots,|\varphi_{m}\rangle in ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}. A basis for ℋn\mathcal{H}_{n} is the set of states

|I⟩=ci1†ci2†⋯cin†|0⟩|I\rangle=c_{i_{1}}^{\dagger}c_{i_{2}}^{\dagger}\cdots c_{i_{n}}^{\dagger}|0\rangle (5)

where I={i1<i2<⋯<in}⊂{1,…,m}I=\{i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{n}\}\subset\{1,\ldots,m\}. A general Slater determinant can be expressed in terms of an m×nm\times n matrix UU with U†​U=1U^{\dagger}U=1 via

|S⟩=d1†⋯dn†|0⟩,di†=∑j=1mUj​icj†.|S\rangle=d_{1}^{\dagger}\cdots d_{n}^{\dagger}|0\rangle,\qquad d_{i}^{\dagger}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}U_{ji}c_{j}^{\dagger}. (6)

The amplitudes of |S⟩|S\rangle are given by ⟨I|S⟩=detU[I,:]\langle I|S\rangle=\det U[I,:] where U[I,:]U[I,:] is the n×nn\times n submatrix on rows II.

In the classical setting, we will assume efficient query access to the amplitudes ⟨S|ψ⟩\langle S|\psi\rangle of the pure state |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle (leaving the mixed state access model to Appendix B). We will also assume few-body observables such as Tr⁡(ci†​cj​ρ)\Tr(c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{j}\rho) are efficiently estimable: that is, we can efficiently sample a random variable XOX_{O} such that 𝔼⁡[XO]=Tr⁡(O​ρ)\mathbb{E}[X_{O}]=\Tr(O\rho) and Var⁡[XO]\mathrm{Var}[X_{O}] is constant and bounded, for few-body observables OO. This is a model for a succinct classical description such as a tensor network or neural quantum state with possibly stochastic estimation. In the quantum setting, we will assume access to quantum copies of the state ρ\rho and the ability to perform arbitrary measurements. In both the classical and quantum settings, the first step will be to estimate the 1-RDM

γi​j=Tr⁡(cj†​ci​ρ),\gamma_{ij}=\Tr(c_{j}^{\dagger}c_{i}\rho), (7)

which is an m×mm\times m matrix. For either a classical noisy estimator or a quantum tomography protocol, this can be achieved within operator norm error η\eta with poly⁡(m,1/η)\mathrm{poly}(m,1/\eta) runtime or measurements [76, 18]. We will find that η=O⁡(ε/n)\eta=O(\varepsilon/n) suffices for later purposes, where ε\varepsilon is the final additive error in Eq. (2), so poly⁡(m,n,1/ε)\mathrm{poly}(m,n,1/\varepsilon) measurements suffice overall.

We begin by describing the classical algorithm for learning the closest Slater, which has three stages: estimating the 1-RDM, diagonalizing it and restricting to an active space, and searching over the active space Slaters. For the first stage, writing γ^\hat{\gamma} as the estimator for γ\gamma, we perform an orthonormal eigendecomposition

γ^i​j=∑a=1mν^a​(ψ^ia)∗​ψ^ja,\hat{\gamma}_{ij}=\sum_{a=1}^{m}\hat{\nu}_{a}(\hat{\psi}_{i}^{a})^{*}\hat{\psi}_{j}^{a}, (8)

which gives us an approximate natural basis ψ^a\hat{\psi}^{a} for ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}. The eigenvalues 0≤ν^a≤10\leq\hat{\nu}_{a}\leq 1 are occupations of the natural orbitals ψ^a\hat{\psi}^{a}.

The next step is to truncate to ψ^a\hat{\psi}^{a} with nontrivial occupations ν^a\hat{\nu}_{a} to isolate an active space 𝒜⊂ℋ1\mathcal{A}\subset\mathcal{H}_{1}. This step mirrors the routine practice of finding an active space in quantum chemistry and electronic structure calculations [67, 55, 50, 43], though it is simpler here. In particular, we choose 𝒜\mathcal{A} to be

𝒜=span⁡{ψ^a∣ν^a>3​ε/8​n}.\mathcal{A}=\mathrm{span}\{\hat{\psi}^{a}\mid\hat{\nu}_{a}>3\varepsilon/8n\}. (9)

If dim𝒜<n\dim\mathcal{A}<n, we enlarge 𝒜\mathcal{A} by adding arbitrary orthonormal orbitals until dim𝒜=n\dim\mathcal{A}=n without loss of generality. In Lemmas 4 and 5 in the Appendix, we prove that it suffices to restrict our attention to 𝒜\mathcal{A} instead of the entire space ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}, incurring at most an ε/2\varepsilon/2 additive error in the objective 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT}, leaving ε/2\varepsilon/2 for the next step. We illustrate this schematically in Fig. 2a. If ‖γ^−γ‖≤ε/8​n\|\hat{\gamma}-\gamma\|\leq\varepsilon/8n, Lemma 5 implies 22 2 before padding, and the same holds after padding for 0<ε≤10<\varepsilon\leq 1.

dim𝒜≤min⁡(m,4​n2ε),\dim\mathcal{A}\leq\min\left(m,\frac{4n^{2}}{\varepsilon}\right), (10)

which is advantageous when n2/ε≪mn^{2}/\varepsilon\ll m. If this condition fails to hold, the truncation to 𝒜\mathcal{A} does not result in appreciable complexity savings and is not necessary. We’ll assume n2/ε≪mn^{2}/\varepsilon\ll m from here on, and thus dim𝒜=O⁡(n2/ε)\dim\mathcal{A}=O(n^{2}/\varepsilon). It remains to optimize the fidelity over this space, which we accomplish below (with the mixed-state generalization in Appendix B).

Theorem 1 (Learning the closest Slater determinant, the classical setting).

Let ρ=|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|\rho=|\psi\rangle\!\langle\psi| be an nn-particle fermionic state. Assume we have an estimator γ^\hat{\gamma} for the 1-RDM γi​j=Tr⁡(cj†​ci​ρ)\gamma_{ij}=\Tr(c_{j}^{\dagger}c_{i}\rho) satisfying ‖γ^−γ‖<ε/8​n\|\hat{\gamma}-\gamma\|<\varepsilon/8n, together with classical query access to the amplitudes ⟨S|ψ⟩\langle S|\psi\rangle. Then we can find the closest Slater to ρ\rho, as measured by fidelity, to an additive error ε\varepsilon in time exp⁡[O⁡(n3ε​log⁡nε)]\exp\!\left[O\!\left(\frac{n^{3}}{\varepsilon}\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon}\right)\right] on a classical computer.

Proof.

By Lemmas 4 and 5, we may restrict the search to Slaters whose occupied orbitals lie in 𝒜\mathcal{A} at the cost of an additive ε/2\varepsilon/2 error in the fidelity:

𝖮𝖯𝖳≤𝖮𝖯𝖳𝒜+ε/2,𝖮𝖯𝖳𝒜=max|S⟩∈𝒮𝒜⁡⟨S|ρ|S⟩.\mathsf{OPT}\leq\mathsf{OPT}_{\mathcal{A}}+\varepsilon/2,\quad\mathsf{OPT}_{\mathcal{A}}=\max_{|S\rangle\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{A}}}\langle S|\rho|S\rangle. (11)

Here, 𝒮𝒜\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{A}} is the manifold of Slater determinants built from orbitals in 𝒜\mathcal{A}. We will bound dim𝒜\dim\mathcal{A} and then consider a covering net over 𝒮𝒜\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{A}}.

We recall that the active subspace 𝒜\mathcal{A} consists of eigenvectors of γ^\hat{\gamma} with eigenvalues >3​ε/8​n>3\varepsilon/8n. For any |u⟩∈𝒜|u\rangle\in\mathcal{A}, we have ⟨u|γ|u⟩≥⟨u|γ^|u⟩−‖γ^−γ‖=3​ε/8​n−ε/8​n=ε/4​n\langle u|\gamma|u\rangle\geq\langle u|\hat{\gamma}|u\rangle-\|\hat{\gamma}-\gamma\|=3\varepsilon/8n-\varepsilon/8n=\varepsilon/4n. Summing over an orthonormal basis of 𝒜\mathcal{A} gives tr⁡γ≥r​ε/4​n\operatorname{tr}\gamma\geq r\varepsilon/4n where r≔dim𝒜r\coloneqq\dim\mathcal{A}, and hence r<4​n2/ε=O⁡(n2/ε)r<4n^{2}/\varepsilon=O(n^{2}/\varepsilon).

We will parameterize each |S⟩∈𝒮𝒜|S\rangle\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{A}} by an r×nr\times n matrix UU with orthonormal columns. We denote this as |S⁡(U)⟩|S(U)\rangle and the fidelity as

F⁡(U)=⟨S⁡(U)|ρ|S⁡(U)⟩.\mathrm{F}(U)=\langle S(U)|\rho|S(U)\rangle. (12)

It will be necessary to bound |F⁡(U)−F⁡(V)||\mathrm{F}(U)-\mathrm{F}(V)| in terms of the difference ‖U−V‖F\|U-V\|_{F} (in Frobenius norm) for two matrices U,VU,V. One can show 33 3 Letting A=|S⁡(U)⟩,B=|S⁡(V)⟩A=|S(U)\rangle,B=|S(V)\rangle, we have |F⁡(U)−F⁡(V)|=|⟨A−B|ρ⁡|A⟩+⟨B|​ρ|A−B⟩|≤|A−B​‖‖ρ‖op​‖A​‖+‖B‖‖​ρ‖op‖​A−B|=2​‖A−B‖|\mathrm{F}(U)-\mathrm{F}(V)|=|\langle A-B|\rho|A\rangle+\langle B|\rho|A-B\rangle|\leq\|A-B\|\|\rho\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|A\|+\|B\|\|\rho\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|A-B\|=2\|A-B\|, since ‖ρ‖op≤1\|\rho\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 1 and ‖A‖=‖B‖=1\|A\|=\|B\|=1.

|F⁡(U)−F⁡(V)|≤2​‖|S⁡(U)⟩−|S⁡(V)⟩‖.|\mathrm{F}(U)-\mathrm{F}(V)|\leq 2\||S(U)\rangle-|S(V)\rangle\|. (13)

We must next bound ‖|S⁡(U)⟩−|S⁡(V)⟩‖\||S(U)\rangle-|S(V)\rangle\| in terms of ‖U−V‖F\|U-V\|_{F}. We write

|S⁡(U)⟩=|u1⟩∧⋯∧|un⟩|S(U)\rangle=|u_{1}\rangle\wedge\cdots\wedge|u_{n}\rangle (14)

where |uk⟩|u_{k}\rangle corresponds to the kk’th column of UU viewed as a single-particle orbital, and similarly for |S⁡(V)⟩|S(V)\rangle. We claim

‖|S⁡(U)⟩−|S⁡(V)⟩‖≤∑k=1n‖|uk⟩−|vk⟩‖\||S(U)\rangle-|S(V)\rangle\|\leq\sum_{k=1}^{n}\||u_{k}\rangle-|v_{k}\rangle\| (15)

and establish this by induction on nn. For n=1n=1, this is true as an equation. For n≥2n\geq 2, we assume it is true for n−1n-1 and we add and subtract [⋀k=1n−1|vk⟩]∧|un⟩\left[\bigwedge_{k=1}^{n-1}|v_{k}\rangle\right]\wedge|u_{n}\rangle, yielding

|S⁡(U)⟩−|S⁡(V)⟩=[⋀k=1n−1|uk⟩−⋀k=1n−1|vk⟩]∧|un⟩+[⋀k=1n−1|vk⟩]∧(|un⟩−|vn⟩).|S(U)\rangle-|S(V)\rangle=\left[\bigwedge_{k=1}^{n-1}|u_{k}\rangle-\bigwedge_{k=1}^{n-1}|v_{k}\rangle\right]\wedge|u_{n}\rangle\\ +\left[\bigwedge_{k=1}^{n-1}|v_{k}\rangle\right]\wedge(|u_{n}\rangle-|v_{n}\rangle). (16)

Taking norms and applying the triangle inequality, we have

‖|S⁡(U)⟩−|S⁡(V)⟩‖\displaystyle\||S(U)\rangle-|S(V)\rangle\| ≤‖⋀k=1n−1|uk⟩−⋀k=1n−1|vk⟩‖​‖|un⟩‖\displaystyle\leq\left\|\bigwedge_{k=1}^{n-1}|u_{k}\rangle-\bigwedge_{k=1}^{n-1}|v_{k}\rangle\right\|\||u_{n}\rangle\|
+‖⋀k=1n−1|vk⟩‖​‖|un⟩−|vn⟩‖\displaystyle+\left\|\bigwedge_{k=1}^{n-1}|v_{k}\rangle\right\|\||u_{n}\rangle-|v_{n}\rangle\| (17)
≤∑k=1n−1‖|uk⟩−|vk⟩‖+‖|un⟩−|vn⟩‖\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\||u_{k}\rangle-|v_{k}\rangle\|+\||u_{n}\rangle-|v_{n}\rangle\|

where we used the inductive hypothesis and ∥∧k=1n−1|uk⟩∥≤∏k=1n−1∥|uk⟩∥=1\|\wedge_{k=1}^{n-1}|u_{k}\rangle\|\leq\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\||u_{k}\rangle\|=1. This establishes Eq. (15). Next, we note that ‖U−V‖F2=∑k=1n‖|uk⟩−|vk⟩‖2\|U-V\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\||u_{k}\rangle-|v_{k}\rangle\|^{2}, which implies ‖|uk⟩−|vk⟩‖≤‖U−V‖F\||u_{k}\rangle-|v_{k}\rangle\|\leq\|U-V\|_{F} for each kk. Combining from Eq. (13), we have

|F⁡(U)−F⁡(V)|≤2​n​‖U−V‖F.|\mathrm{F}(U)-\mathrm{F}(V)|\leq 2n\|U-V\|_{F}. (18)

Next, we consider a covering of 𝒮𝒜\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{A}}, which is a compact manifold of real dimension d=2​n​(r−n)d=2n(r-n), as illustrated heuristically in Fig. 2b. It hence admits a δ\delta-covering net with (c/δ)d(c/\delta)^{d} elements for some constant cc [57]. We take δ=ε/4​n\delta=\varepsilon/4n so that every |S⁡(U)⟩|S(U)\rangle has a net point |S⁡(U′)⟩|S(U^{\prime})\rangle such that ‖U−U′‖F<ε/4​n\|U-U^{\prime}\|_{F}<\varepsilon/4n and hence |F⁡(U)−F⁡(U′)|≤ε/2|\mathrm{F}(U)-\mathrm{F}(U^{\prime})|\leq\varepsilon/2. The net has number of elements

(4​n​cε)2​n​(r−n)=exp⁡[O⁡(n3ε​log⁡nε)]\left(\frac{4nc}{\varepsilon}\right)^{2n(r-n)}=\exp\left[O\left(\frac{n^{3}}{\varepsilon}\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon}\right)\right] (19)

where we used r=O⁡(n2/ε)r=O(n^{2}/\varepsilon). We then enumerate this net, evaluate F at each point, and return a Slater with maximum fidelity among all net points. Let |S⁡(U′)⟩|S(U^{\prime})\rangle be the corresponding Slater and |S⁡(U⋆)⟩|S(U^{\star})\rangle be a true maximum over all 𝒮𝒜\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{A}}. Then

F⁡(U′)≥F⁡(U⋆)−ε/2=𝖮𝖯𝖳𝒜−ε/2≥𝖮𝖯𝖳−ε,\mathrm{F}(U^{\prime})\geq\mathrm{F}(U^{\star})-\varepsilon/2=\mathsf{OPT}_{\mathcal{A}}-\varepsilon/2\geq\mathsf{OPT}-\varepsilon, (20)

using Eq. (11). This procedure hence returns an optimal Slater to within an additive ε\varepsilon tolerance, as desired. ∎

It is worth clarifying why the covering net search of Theorem 1 may be necessary in general. Having isolated the active space from the 1-RDM, one might hope to avoid the covering net search and simply occupy the nn natural orbitals of largest occupation, returning the resulting Slater. This approach succeeds when ρ\rho is a Slater and may be accurate when the 1-RDM eigenvalues lie close to either 00 or 11, but it can fail badly in general. In other words, the closest Slater is not a simple function of the 1-RDM alone. For example, consider the state

|ψ⟩=13​(c1†​c2†​c3†+c3†​c4†​c5†+c5†​c6†​c1†)​|0⟩.|\psi\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\left(c_{1}^{\dagger}c_{2}^{\dagger}c_{3}^{\dagger}+c_{3}^{\dagger}c_{4}^{\dagger}c_{5}^{\dagger}+c_{5}^{\dagger}c_{6}^{\dagger}c_{1}^{\dagger}\right)|0\rangle. (21)

Each pair of terms differs in two orbitals, so the 1-RDM is diagonal, with occupation 2/32/3 on orbitals 1,3,51,3,5 and 1/31/3 on orbitals 2,4,62,4,6. The Slater corresponding to the three leading occupations in the 1-RDM is thus c1†​c3†​c5†​|0⟩c_{1}^{\dagger}c_{3}^{\dagger}c_{5}^{\dagger}|0\rangle, which has zero overlap with |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle, while the true closest Slater fidelity satisfies 𝖮𝖯𝖳≥1/3\mathsf{OPT}\geq 1/3 (taking e.g. c1†​c2†​c3†​|0⟩c_{1}^{\dagger}c_{2}^{\dagger}c_{3}^{\dagger}|0\rangle). Indeed, there is no efficient (polynomial in n,1/εn,1/\varepsilon) protocol for determining the closest Slater from the 1-RDM alone in general under certain computational complexity assumptions, as we detail in Sec. IV.

In conclusion, the classical algorithm presented here gives an answer to the question posed at the beginning of the paper in its precise form (Eq. (2)). We turn to the quantum setting next.

III Quantum setting

We turn to the problem of learning the closest Slater under the assumptions of the quantum access model. In particular, we assume access to quantum copies of the state ρ\rho with the ability to make arbitrary measurements. We design an algorithm with poly⁡(n,1/ε)\mathrm{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon) sample complexity, independent of mm, using the active space estimate; identifying the active space may incur a separate poly⁡(m,n,1/ε)\mathrm{poly}(m,n,1/\varepsilon) overhead, as we discuss. The runtime remains exponential in poly⁡(n,1/ε)\mathrm{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon). We leave open the question of whether a subexponential-in-nn runtime is possible.

Our protocol makes use of the quantum threshold search (QTS) algorithm of Badescu and O’Donnell [6]. Let us review the relevant parts. Let ρ\rho be an unknown quantum state and A1,…,AMA_{1},\ldots,A_{M} observables satisfying 0⪯Ai⪯10\preceq A_{i}\preceq 1 44 4 where A⪯BA\preceq B means B−AB-A is positive semidefinite and let θ1,…,θM∈[0,1]\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{M}\in[0,1]. Given a desired accuracy ε>0\varepsilon>0 and a tolerable failure probability δ>0\delta>0, Ref. [6] provides an algorithm using

nQTS=O⁡(1ε2​(log2⁡M+log⁡1δ)​log⁡1δ)n_{\mathrm{QTS}}=O\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{2}}\left(\log^{2}M+\log\frac{1}{\delta}\right)\log\frac{1}{\delta}\right) (22)

copies of ρ\rho which, except with probability at most δ\delta, either returns an index jj such that Tr⁡(ρ​Aj)>θj−ε\Tr(\rho A_{j})>\theta_{j}-\varepsilon or certifies that Tr⁡(ρ​Aj)<θj\Tr(\rho A_{j})<\theta_{j} for all jj. We will apply this primitive to the projectors onto a finite net of Slater determinants (c.f. Fig. 2, Theorem 1). The noteworthy feature is the log2⁡M\log^{2}M dependence, which is exponentially better than the Ω⁡(M)\Omega(M) copies a naïve search over the MM candidates would require.

We will need to slightly generalize the quantum threshold search algorithm to also search over the thresholds θ1,…,θM\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{M}. In fact, we will set them to be all equal (θ=θ1=⋯=θM\theta=\theta_{1}=\cdots=\theta_{M}) and perform a binary search over θ∈[0,1]\theta\in[0,1]. The final value of θ\theta will satisfy |θ−𝖮𝖯𝖳|<ε|\theta-\mathsf{OPT}|<\varepsilon. This is achieved by the following Lemma, whose proof is left to Appendix C.

Lemma 9 (Agnostic quantum threshold search) Let A1,…,AMA_{1},\ldots,A_{M} be known observables with 0⪯Ai⪯10\preceq A_{i}\preceq 1 and let Fi≔Tr⁡(ρ​Ai)F_{i}\coloneqq\Tr(\rho A_{i}) and F⋆=maxi⁡FiF_{\star}=\max_{i}F_{i}. Given quantum copies of ρ\rho, there is a procedure which outputs an index i⋆i_{\star} such that Fi⋆≥F⋆−εF_{i_{\star}}\geq F_{\star}-\varepsilon with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, using

nAQTS=O⁡(με2​(log2⁡M+log⁡μδ)​log⁡μδ)n_{\mathrm{AQTS}}=O\left(\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon^{2}}\left(\log^{2}M+\log\frac{\mu}{\delta}\right)\log\frac{\mu}{\delta}\right) (23)

copies of ρ\rho, where μ≔log⁡(1/ε)\mu\coloneqq\log(1/\varepsilon).

We will apply agnostic QTS to the problem of learning the closest Slater determinant in the quantum setting. This is presented formally in the following Theorem, depicted schematically in Fig. 2c.

Theorem 2 (Learning the closest Slater determinant, the quantum setting).

Let ρ\rho be an arbitrary nn-fermion state and suppose we have an estimator γ^\hat{\gamma} for the 1-RDM γ\gamma satisfying ‖γ^−γ‖≤ε12​n\|\hat{\gamma}-\gamma\|\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{12n}. Suppose for each explicitly specified Slater determinant |S⟩|S\rangle we can implement the two-outcome measurement {|S⟩​⟨S|,1−|S⟩​⟨S|}\{|S\rangle\!\langle S|,1-|S\rangle\!\langle S|\}. Then there is a quantum protocol which outputs a Slater determinant |S⋆⟩|S^{\star}\rangle satisfying ⟨S⋆|ρ|S⋆⟩≥𝖮𝖯𝖳−ε\langle S^{\star}|\rho|S^{\star}\rangle\geq\mathsf{OPT}-\varepsilon with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, using

N=O~​(n6ε4)N=\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{n^{6}}{\varepsilon^{4}}\right) (24)

copies of ρ\rho, where O~\widetilde{O} omits logarithmic factors in n,1/ε,n,1/\varepsilon, and 1/δ1/\delta. The runtime is exponential in poly⁡(n,1/ε)\mathrm{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon).

Proof.

From the 1-RDM estimator satisfying ‖γ^−γ‖≤ε12​n\|\hat{\gamma}-\gamma\|\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{12n}, we perform an eigendecomposition γ^i​j=∑a=1mν^a​(ψ^ia)∗​ψ^ja\hat{\gamma}_{ij}=\sum_{a=1}^{m}\hat{\nu}_{a}(\hat{\psi}_{i}^{a})^{*}\hat{\psi}_{j}^{a} and define an active space 𝒜=span⁡{ψ^a∣ν^a>ε/4​n}.\mathcal{A}=\mathrm{span}\{\hat{\psi}^{a}\mid\hat{\nu}_{a}>\varepsilon/4n\}. Then, for |v⟩∈𝒜⟂|v\rangle\in\mathcal{A}^{\perp} we have ⟨v|γ|v⟩≤⟨v|γ^|v⟩+|γ^−γ|=ε/3​n\langle v|\gamma|v\rangle\leq\langle v|\hat{\gamma}|v\rangle+\|\hat{\gamma}-\gamma\|=\varepsilon/3n and Lemma 4 gives 𝖮𝖯𝖳≤𝖮𝖯𝖳𝒜+ε/3\mathsf{OPT}\leq\mathsf{OPT}_{\mathcal{A}}+\varepsilon/3. Moreover, r≔dim𝒜≤6​n2/ε=O⁡(n2/ε)r\coloneqq\dim\mathcal{A}\leq 6n^{2}/\varepsilon=O(n^{2}/\varepsilon) as before. We assume an ε\varepsilon-covering net of 𝒮𝒜\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{A}} is chosen as in Theorem 1, and we refer there for further details. Our strategy will be to apply agnostic quantum threshold search to the family of Slater projectors in this covering net.

In particular, we choose a net whose constituents have radius ε/6​n\varepsilon/6n, which covers the manifold 𝒮𝒜\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{A}} with fidelity accuracy ε/3\varepsilon/3. We denote this as {|S1⟩,…,|SM⟩}\{|S_{1}\rangle,\ldots,|S_{M}\rangle\} with

M≤(6​n​cε)2​n​(r−n)M\leq\left(\frac{6nc}{\varepsilon}\right)^{2n(r-n)} (25)

where cc is the same constant appearing in Eq. (19). For each kk, let Ak=|Sk⟩​⟨Sk|A_{k}=|S_{k}\rangle\!\langle S_{k}|. We apply Lemma 9 to A1,…,AMA_{1},\ldots,A_{M} with accuracy ε/3\varepsilon/3. In the event of no failures, this procedure returns i⋆i_{\star} where |S⋆⟩≔|Si⋆⟩|S^{\star}\rangle\coloneqq|S_{i_{\star}}\rangle satisfies

⟨S⋆|ρ|S⋆⟩≥maxk⁡⟨Sk|ρ|Sk⟩−ε/3.\langle S^{\star}|\rho|S^{\star}\rangle\geq\max_{k}\langle S_{k}|\rho|S_{k}\rangle-\varepsilon/3. (26)

By design of the net, we have maxk⁡⟨Sk|ρ|Sk⟩≥𝖮𝖯𝖳𝒜−ε/3\max_{k}\langle S_{k}|\rho|S_{k}\rangle\geq\mathsf{OPT}_{\mathcal{A}}-\varepsilon/3. Moreover, by our choice of 𝒜\mathcal{A} we have 𝖮𝖯𝖳𝒜≥𝖮𝖯𝖳−ε/3\mathsf{OPT}_{\mathcal{A}}\geq\mathsf{OPT}-\varepsilon/3. Combining these inequalities, we have

⟨S⋆|ρ|S⋆⟩≥𝖮𝖯𝖳−ε.\langle S^{\star}|\rho|S^{\star}\rangle\geq\mathsf{OPT}-\varepsilon. (27)

Finally, combining r=O⁡(n2/ε)r=O(n^{2}/\varepsilon) with log⁡M=O⁡(n⁡(r−n)​log⁡(n/ε))\log M=O\left(n(r-n)\log(n/\varepsilon)\right) and substituting into nAQTSn_{\mathrm{AQTS}} (Eq. (23)) yields N=O~​(n6/ε4)N=\widetilde{O}\left(n^{6}/\varepsilon^{4}\right), as was to be shown. ∎

In Theorem 2, we have assumed the estimator γ^\hat{\gamma} was given. In practice, γ^\hat{\gamma} must be constructed using tomography on ρ\rho, and we must count the number of copies of ρ\rho needed for this step of the procedure. We account for this using Lemma 5, which establishes using fermionic classical shadows [76, 70, 18] that an estimator γ^\hat{\gamma} for the 1-RDM γ\gamma satisfying ‖γ^−γ‖≤η\|\hat{\gamma}-\gamma\|\leq\eta can be found with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta using nfcs=O⁡(m2​log⁡(m/δ)η2)n_{\mathrm{fcs}}=O\left(\frac{m^{2}\log(m/\delta)}{\eta^{2}}\right) quantum copies of ρ\rho. In the context of the previous theorem, we need η∼ε/n\eta\sim\varepsilon/n, and hence the sample complexity from this estimation stage is O⁡(m2​n2​log⁡(m/δ)ε2)=poly⁡(m,n,1/ε)O\left(\frac{m^{2}n^{2}\log(m/\delta)}{\varepsilon^{2}}\right)=\mathrm{poly}(m,n,1/\varepsilon).

At this stage, we have provided algorithms for learning the closest Slater in both the classical and quantum access models. These correspond to the upper bounds in Table 1. Next, we turn to computational hardness lower bounds, which limit the possible efficiency of any algorithm for this problem.

IV Computational hardness

So far, we have provided algorithms for learning the closest Slater determinant whose time complexities are polynomial in mm, the single-particle Hilbert space dimension, at constant particle number nn and additive error ε\varepsilon. However, they are exponential in poly⁡(n,1/ε)\mathrm{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon) at fixed mm. In this section, we establish computational hardness lower bounds in both nn and 1/ε1/\varepsilon based on standard complexity-theoretic assumptions, hence showing that this time complexity cannot be substantially improved along either axis, albeit with one substantive problem left open: the possibility of subexponential dependence in nn for a quantum algorithm. In the classical case, the following results render our upper bound essentially time-optimal. Figure 3 summarizes the two hardness reductions and the resulting complexity landscape.

IV.1 Classical hardness in particle number

First, we prove a hardness lower bound in nn for the classical setting. To prove this, we will use a standard hardness assumption from parameterized complexity, namely the hardness of the nn-Multicolored Clique problem [20]. In this problem, one is given a graph whose vertices are partitioned into nn colors

V1,…,Vn,V_{1},\ldots,V_{n}, (28)

with each subset of size pp, for a total of n​pnp vertices. A Multicolored Clique is a choice of one vertex per color such that the nn chosen vertices are pairwise connected. Under the standard exponential time hypothesis (ETH), one does not expect an algorithm running in time f⁡(n)​po⁡(n)f(n)p^{o(n)} for this problem, for any computable ff.

For our purposes, it is convenient to use a variation where the graph is guaranteed to have zero or one multicolored clique. This is without any significant loss of generality due to the Valiant-Vazirani theorem [64]. One detail of appealing to this theorem is that we will phrase our assumption in the more general setting of randomized algorithms. Our self-contained assumption, therefore, will be as follows.

Assumption 1 (nn-Multicolored Clique [20, 64]).

Let GG be an nn-colored graph, with each color class of size pp. Given GG, there is no randomized algorithm running in time f⁡(n)​po⁡(n)f(n)p^{o(n)}, for any computable function ff, which distinguishes the following two cases (with success probability bounded above 1/21/2 by a constant) under the promise that one is true:

  1. 1.

    GG has no nn-multicolored clique

  2. 2.

    GG has exactly one nn-multicolored clique.

Under this assumption, we prove the following:

Theorem 3 (Classical complexity lower bound).

Fix any λ<1\lambda<1. Under Assumption 1, there exists a constant ελ>0\varepsilon_{\lambda}>0 such that no randomized algorithm running in time f⁡(n)​mo⁡(n)f(n)m^{o(n)} can solve the following task in general: given a succinct classical description of a nonzero nn-fermion vector |Φ⟩|\Phi\rangle on mm modes, output a Slater |S⟩|S\rangle satisfying

|⟨S|Φ⟩|2‖Φ‖2≥𝖮𝖯𝖳−ελ,\frac{|\langle S|\Phi\rangle|^{2}}{\|\Phi\|^{2}}\geq\mathsf{OPT}-\varepsilon_{\lambda}, (29)

where 𝖮𝖯𝖳=max|S⟩∈𝒮⁡|⟨S|Φ⟩|2/‖Φ‖2\mathsf{OPT}=\max_{|S\rangle\in\mathcal{S}}|\langle S|\Phi\rangle|^{2}/\|\Phi\|^{2}, with success probability at least 0.990.99, even under the promise that 𝖮𝖯𝖳≥λ.\mathsf{OPT}\geq\lambda. Here a succinct classical description means a polynomial-size circuit which, on inputting a set I⊂[m]I\subset[m] with corresponding Slater determinant |I⟩|I\rangle, returns the (possibly unnormalized) amplitude ⟨I|Φ⟩\langle I|\Phi\rangle.

Below we outline the main ideas of the proof, leaving the full argument to Appendix A.1. We embed the nn-Multicolored Clique problem inside a fermionic state, as shown schematically in Fig. 3b. Let GG be an nn-colored graph satisfying the promise of Assumption 1. It will be slightly more convenient to have the promise of either one or two nn-multicolored cliques, so we add to GG a disjoint clique DD and then assign one fermionic mode to each vertex. The fermionic state is chosen as |ΦG⟩=|D⟩+α⁡|C⟩|\Phi_{G}\rangle=|D\rangle+\alpha|C\rangle, with α>1\alpha>1. Here, |C⟩|C\rangle is the Slater for the hidden clique if it exists and |C⟩=0|C\rangle=0 otherwise. The state |ΦG⟩|\Phi_{G}\rangle has a succinct description, since each amplitude ⟨I|ΦG⟩\langle I|\Phi_{G}\rangle equals 1,α,1,\alpha, or 00 and can be computed from the graph in O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) time. Because DD and CC share no orbitals, the closest Slater is |C⟩|C\rangle when it exists and |D⟩|D\rangle otherwise (Lemma 6). Taking a single overlap with |D⟩|D\rangle then reveals the solution to nn-Multicolored Clique. Hence, an efficient closest Slater algorithm would violate Assumption 1.

This establishes that the classical time complexity cannot be substantially improved beyond the one presented in Sec. II, and in particular no subexponential-in-nn algorithm should be expected. We note that this argument is based on a classical access model. Our quantum algorithm also has exponential-in-nn runtime, but the argument above does not provide a lower bound in the quantum setting.

IV.2 Hardness in precision

A second axis of computational hardness is the scaling with respect to the precision ε\varepsilon. Here, we show that the exponential 1/ε1/\varepsilon scaling in the time complexity of the classical and quantum algorithms cannot be improved to polynomial when we allow the input state to be mixed, based on widely-believed complexity-theoretic assumptions. In particular, we prove the following theorem, shown schematically in Fig. 3c.

Theorem 4 (Computational hardness).

There exists a positive constant cc such that if there exists a poly⁡(m)\mathrm{poly}(m)-time quantum algorithm that takes as input the classical description of any (possibly mixed) density matrix ρ\rho of n=2n=2 fermions on mm modes and outputs a Slater determinant |S⟩∈𝒮|S\rangle\in\mathcal{S} satisfying

⟨S|ρ|S⟩≥𝖮𝖯𝖳−1/mc\langle S|\rho|S\rangle\geq\mathsf{OPT}-1/m^{c} (30)

with probability at least 2/32/3, then 𝖭𝖯⊆𝖡𝖰𝖯\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}. Moreover, if such a randomized classical algorithm exists, then 𝖭𝖯⊆𝖡𝖯𝖯\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{BPP}.

In particular, this proved absence of poly⁡(m)\mathrm{poly}(m)-time algorithms implies the absence of poly⁡(1/ε)\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon) algorithms, by choosing ε=1/mc\varepsilon=1/m^{c}. Hence, we have the (1/ε)ω⁡(1)(1/\varepsilon)^{\omega(1)} runtime lower bound quoted in Table 1.

We outline the main idea of the proof, leaving the full argument to Appendix A.2. The basic idea is to reduce the problem to the quantum separability problem, which asks whether a bipartite quantum state ρ\rho is entangled or separable. When ρ\rho is located within an inverse polynomial (with respect to dimension) distance from the border of the set of separable quantum states, this problem was shown to be 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-hard [26]. To relate this problem with learning Slater determinants, we may regard two fermions in an even number of modes mm as two fermions in m/2m/2 modes with opposite spins, and the Slater fidelity of the former corresponds to the separability of the latter when the spin degree of freedom is anti-symmetrized. In this case, the “spatial” wavefunction of the fermions in a Slater determinant state is in a product state. This gives a reduction between testing separability and the problem of learning the closest Slater determinant. This hardness applies to both the classical and quantum access models; indeed, even if we have access to the complete classical description of the density matrix, solving the closest Slater problem will take superpolynomial time in 1/ε1/\varepsilon unless 𝖭𝖯⊆𝖡𝖯𝖯/𝖡𝖰𝖯\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{BPP}/\mathsf{BQP}, which is widely believed to be false.

V Optimization landscape

So far, we have assumed that the fermionic state |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle is arbitrary. In this section, we study the situation where |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle is already known to be close to a Slater determinant. Loosely speaking, this corresponds to |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle being weakly correlated, and hence still captures many interesting quantum systems including filled-valence molecules and weakly interacting phases of matter. Our specific result is the following. Suppose that we have a trial Slater |G⟩|G\rangle satisfying |⟨G|ψ⟩|2>2/3|\langle G|\psi\rangle|^{2}>2/3; then |G⟩|G\rangle is close to the optimal Slater determinant, in a manner to be made precise. This guarantee is useful for a non-convex optimization problem and is noteworthy for its independence of m,nm,n, or model details.

Practically, this result could prove useful in the following scenario. Suppose we have a heuristic algorithm to find the closest Slater, such as gradient ascent or Hartree-Fock-style iteration. If we arrive at a Slater determinant |G⟩|G\rangle with fidelity F>2/3\mathrm{F}>2/3, then it suffices to perform some local optimization to refine the ansätz |G⟩|G\rangle into the globally closest Slater determinant. In particular, if |G⟩|G\rangle satisfies a further stationarity condition, to be defined, then |G⟩|G\rangle is globally optimal. Since the original problem is a non-convex optimization, for which a local optimum need not be a global one, this guarantee can prove valuable. We will also prove that this condition cannot be improved, in the sense that the constant 2/32/3 is optimal in general.

To proceed, let |G⟩|G\rangle be an arbitrary Slater and choose an orthonormal basis g1,…,gng_{1},\ldots,g_{n} such that |G⟩=cg1†⋯cgn†|0⟩|G\rangle=c_{g_{1}}^{\dagger}\cdots c_{g_{n}}^{\dagger}|0\rangle. Let f1,…,fm−nf_{1},\ldots,f_{m-n} be an orthonormal basis for the unoccupied orbitals and define single-particle-hole excitations

|Ga​μ⟩≔cfa†​cgμ​|G⟩.|G_{a\mu}\rangle\coloneqq c_{f_{a}}^{\dagger}c_{g_{\mu}}|G\rangle. (31)

Let |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle be our fermionic state. We define α=|⟨G|ψ⟩|\alpha=|\langle G|\psi\rangle| and

κ=α−2​1−α2,\kappa=\alpha-\sqrt{2}\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}}, (32)

noting that α2>2/3⇔κ>0\alpha^{2}>2/3\iff\kappa>0. Finally, we define

BG≔∑a​μ|⟨Ga​μ|ψ⟩|2.B_{G}\coloneqq\sqrt{\sum_{a\mu}|\langle G_{a\mu}|\psi\rangle|^{2}}. (33)

By Lemma 7, BG=0B_{G}=0 is precisely the condition that fidelity is stationary with respect to |G⟩|G\rangle. We refer to BGB_{G} as the Brillouin residual [12].

Theorem 5 (2/32/3 certificate).

Let |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle be a normalized fermionic state and let |G⟩|G\rangle be a Slater determinant. Define κ\kappa and BGB_{G} as above. Suppose

|⟨G|ψ⟩|2>2/3|\langle G|\psi\rangle|^{2}>2/3 (34)

and let 𝖮𝖯𝖳=max|S⟩∈𝒮⁡|⟨S|ψ⟩|2\mathsf{OPT}=\max_{|S\rangle\in\mathcal{S}}|\langle S|\psi\rangle|^{2}. Then

𝖮𝖯𝖳≤(|⟨G|ψ⟩|+BG22​κ)2.\mathsf{OPT}\leq\left(|\langle G|\psi\rangle|+\frac{B_{G}^{2}}{2\kappa}\right)^{2}. (35)

In particular, if BG=0B_{G}=0 then |G⟩|G\rangle is the unique globally closest Slater determinant to |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle, up to phase.

We note that 2/32/3 is a worst-case threshold, and is far from tight for typical states. Across various ensembles of random and physical quantum states, we have numerically observed that spurious stationary points only occur at fidelities well below 2/32/3 (Fig. 4c and Sec. VI). As a state-independent guarantee, however, the constant 2/32/3 cannot be improved, as we will show.

Proof of Theorem 5.

Let |H⟩|H\rangle be an arbitrary Slater determinant. We will compare |⟨H|ψ⟩||\langle H|\psi\rangle| to |⟨G|ψ⟩||\langle G|\psi\rangle|. Following the notation of Lemma 8, we decompose |H⟩|H\rangle into particle-hole sectors relative to |G⟩|G\rangle:

|H⟩=|h0⟩+|h1⟩+|h≥2⟩.|H\rangle=|h_{0}\rangle+|h_{1}\rangle+|h_{\geq 2}\rangle. (36)

Here |h0⟩|h_{0}\rangle is proportional to |G⟩|G\rangle, |h1⟩|h_{1}\rangle lies in the single-particle-hole sector spanned by the |Ga​μ⟩|G_{a\mu}\rangle, and |h≥2⟩|h_{\geq 2}\rangle is the remainder. We choose the phase of |H⟩|H\rangle so that |h0⟩=s​|G⟩|h_{0}\rangle=s|G\rangle with s=|⟨H|G⟩|s=|\langle H|G\rangle|, and we’ll write p1:=‖|h1⟩‖2,q2:=‖|h≥2⟩‖2.p_{1}:=\left\||h_{1}\rangle\right\|^{2},q^{2}:=\left\||h_{\geq 2}\rangle\right\|^{2}. We perform the analogous particle-hole decomposition of the target state |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle relative to |G⟩|G\rangle, writing

|ψ⟩=α⁡|G⟩+|ψ1⟩+|ψ≥2⟩,|\psi\rangle=\alpha|G\rangle+|\psi_{1}\rangle+|\psi_{\geq 2}\rangle, (37)

where we’ve absorbed a possible phase into |G⟩|G\rangle and we note ‖|ψ1⟩‖=BG\||\psi_{1}\rangle\|=B_{G}. We also note ‖|ψ≥2⟩‖≤1−α2\||\psi_{\geq 2}\rangle\|\leq\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}}. Using these decompositions and applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to each sector, we find

|⟨H|ψ⟩|≤α​s+BG​p1+1−α2​q.|\langle H|\psi\rangle|\leq\alpha s+B_{G}\sqrt{p_{1}}+\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}}q. (38)

We now make use of two bounds. First, p1≤1−s2≤2​(1−s).p_{1}\leq 1-s^{2}\leq 2(1-s). Second, by Lemma 8, q≤2​(1−s).q\leq\sqrt{2}\,(1-s). Then

|⟨H|ψ⟩|\displaystyle|\langle H|\psi\rangle| ≤α​s+BG​2​(1−s)+2​1−α2​(1−s)\displaystyle\leq\alpha s+B_{G}\sqrt{2(1-s)}+\sqrt{2}\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}}(1-s)
=α−κ⁡(1−s)+BG​2​(1−s).\displaystyle=\alpha-\kappa(1-s)+B_{G}\sqrt{2(1-s)}. (39)

Since κ>0\kappa>0, this expression is uniformly bounded over 0≤s≤10\leq s\leq 1 by

maxs∈[0,1]⁡{α−κ⁡(1−s)+BG​2​(1−s)}≤α+BG22​κ.\max_{s\in[0,1]}\left\{\alpha-\kappa(1-s)+B_{G}\sqrt{2(1-s)}\right\}\leq\alpha+\frac{B_{G}^{2}}{2\kappa}. (40)

Therefore every Slater determinant |H⟩|H\rangle satisfies |⟨H|ψ⟩|≤α+BG22​κ.|\langle H|\psi\rangle|\leq\alpha+\frac{B_{G}^{2}}{2\kappa}. Taking the maximum over |H⟩|H\rangle and squaring proves the claim. For uniqueness, we note that when BG=0B_{G}=0 the prior bound indicates |⟨H|ψ⟩|≤α−κ⁡(1−s)|\langle H|\psi\rangle|\leq\alpha-\kappa(1-s) with κ>0\kappa>0 and s≤1s\leq 1. Since 𝖮𝖯𝖳=α2\mathsf{OPT}=\alpha^{2}, any global maximum |H⟩|H\rangle attains |⟨H|ψ⟩|=α|\langle H|\psi\rangle|=\alpha, forcing κ⁡(1−s)≤0\kappa(1-s)\leq 0 and hence s=1s=1. Thus |H⟩=|G⟩|H\rangle=|G\rangle up to phase. ∎

Corollary 1 (High-fidelity stationary Slaters are optimal).

Let |G⟩|G\rangle be a Slater determinant with |⟨G|ψ⟩|2>2/3.|\langle G|\psi\rangle|^{2}>2/3. If |G⟩|G\rangle is stationary, meaning BG=0,B_{G}=0, then |G⟩|G\rangle is the unique globally closest to |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle, up to phase.

The above theorem motivates the following question: can the threshold of 2/32/3 fidelity be improved? That is, is there a lower number for which the theorem and corollary hold? We answer this in the negative in the theorem below, establishing 2/32/3 as the sharp threshold above which the vanishing of BGB_{G} implies global optimality for the closest Slater determinant problem.

Theorem 6 (Sharpness of the 2/32/3 threshold).

For every c<2/3c<2/3, there exist integers m,nm,n, a normalized nn-fermion state |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle, and a Slater determinant |G⟩|G\rangle such that |⟨G|ψ⟩|2>c|\langle G|\psi\rangle|^{2}>c and BG=0B_{G}=0 but |G⟩|G\rangle is not globally closest to |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle. Hence no m,nm,n-independent statement of the form of Theorem 5 can hold for c<2/3c<2/3.

Proof.

We’ll construct an explicit counterexample. Take m=2​nm=2n fermionic modes with orthonormal orbitals e1,…,en,f1,…,fne_{1},\ldots,e_{n},f_{1},\ldots,f_{n} and let |G⟩=ce1†⋯cen†|0⟩|G\rangle=c_{e_{1}}^{\dagger}\cdots c_{e_{n}}^{\dagger}|0\rangle. For t>0t>0, define the rotated Slater determinant

|Ht⟩=∏i=1ncei†+t​cfi†1+t2​|0⟩.|H_{t}\rangle=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{c_{e_{i}}^{\dagger}+tc_{f_{i}}^{\dagger}}{\sqrt{1+t^{2}}}|0\rangle. (41)

We’ll decompose |Ht⟩|H_{t}\rangle into particle-hole sectors relative to |G⟩|G\rangle:

|Ht⟩=st​|G⟩+|ht,1⟩+|ht,≥2⟩.|H_{t}\rangle=s_{t}|G\rangle+|h_{t,1}\rangle+|h_{t,\geq 2}\rangle. (42)

From explicit calculation, we have st=(1+t2)−n/2s_{t}=(1+t^{2})^{-n/2} and

qt≔‖|ht,≥2⟩‖=[1−(1+n​t2)​st2]1/2.q_{t}\coloneqq\||h_{t,\geq 2}\rangle\|=[1-(1+nt^{2})s_{t}^{2}]^{1/2}. (43)

We also note that limt→0qt1−st=2​(n−1)/n\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{q_{t}}{1-s_{t}}=\sqrt{2(n-1)/n} which approaches 2\sqrt{2} as n→∞n\to\infty. Now choose α\alpha such that c<α2<2/3.c<\alpha^{2}<2/3. Since α2<2/3\alpha^{2}<2/3, we have α1−α2<2.\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}}}<\sqrt{2}. We choose nn large enough and t>0t>0 small enough that qt1−st>α1−α2\frac{q_{t}}{1-s_{t}}>\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}}} and define the state

|ψ⟩=α⁡|G⟩+1−α2qt​|ht,≥2⟩,|\psi\rangle=\alpha|G\rangle+\frac{\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}}}{q_{t}}|h_{t,\geq 2}\rangle, (44)

which is properly normalized, ⟨ψ|ψ⟩=1\langle\psi|\psi\rangle=1. Moreover, |⟨G|ψ⟩|2=α2>c|\langle G|\psi\rangle|^{2}=\alpha^{2}>c and BG=0B_{G}=0, since |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle has no single-particle-hole component relative to |G⟩|G\rangle. However, |G⟩|G\rangle is not the globally closest Slater to |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle; rather, we have

|⟨Ht|ψ⟩|2\displaystyle|\langle H_{t}|\psi\rangle|^{2} =(α​st+1−α2​qt)2\displaystyle=(\alpha s_{t}+\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}}q_{t})^{2} (45)
>(α​st+α⁡(1−st))2=α2\displaystyle>(\alpha s_{t}+\alpha(1-s_{t}))^{2}=\alpha^{2}

so |Ht⟩|H_{t}\rangle is closer. This construction provides the desired counterexample. ∎

We will refer to the states |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle defined above as “adversarial” states, as they are constructed to be adversarially difficult for a closest-Slater algorithm. Together with Theorem 5, the theorem above establishes F=2/3=2/3 as a sharp threshold in the optimization landscape. Above it, every stationary point is the global maximum, while below it, stationary points need not be globally optimal. We have stated these high-fidelity results for pure states for clarity of exposition, but these results extend to the mixed-state setting, with the residual BGB_{G} replaced by a suitable mixed-state analog. Moreover, the algorithmic and hardness results carry over as well. We prove these extensions in Appendix B.

VI Numerical results

In this section, we apply the closest Slater classical algorithm to ground states of interacting fermionic models and characterize the optimization landscape. We summarize results here and leave the details of the numerics to Appendix D. First, we study the Fermi–Hubbard model

H=−t∑⟨i​j⟩,σc†i​σcj​σ+U∑ini↑ni↓H\;=\;-t\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,\sigma}c^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}c_{j\sigma}\;+\;U\sum_{i}n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow} (46)

on an Lx×LyL_{x}\times L_{y} square lattice with (n↑,n↓)(n_{\uparrow},n_{\downarrow}) particles of each spin. At each U/tU/t, we solve for the ground state using exact diagonalization or neural quantum states. We then evaluate 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT} using the classical algorithm described in Sec. II, which involves computing the 1-RDM, restricting to an active space, and searching over a covering net of the corresponding manifold of Slaters. Fig. 1c shows the closest Slater fidelity 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT} of the ground state as a function of |U|/t|U|/t using exact diagonalization. Fig. 4c shows the same result (reproduced) as well as the result using a variationally optimized neural quantum state.

The value of 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT} is unity in the noninteracting limit and decreases as |U||U| grows and correlations build. 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT} decreases more rapidly for attractive interactions, U<0U<0, than for repulsive interactions U>0U>0. This is a manifestation of the pairing correlations of the ground state of the attractive Fermi-Hubbard model, which preclude high-fidelity representation by a Slater determinant.

Our algorithm requires only sample access, as demonstrated in Fig. 4a where 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT} is calculated using Monte Carlo sampling of a neural quantum state (NQS). The NQS representation [14] provides a versatile ansätz for strongly correlated electron wavefunctions and allows Monte Carlo estimation of sparse observables. In practice, NQS have proven competitive across condensed matter, quantum chemistry, and nuclear physics [40, 15, 16, 48, 77, 59, 25, 47, 35, 46, 73, 2, 29, 24]. Motivated by this broad applicability, here we demonstrate that computing 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT} by sampling a NQS can be straightforward and informative. We choose a linear combination of Slater-Jastrow terms as the NQS ansätz, and results are close to ED with the deviation originating from imperfect training and the width originating from Monte Carlo standard deviation.

In Fig. 4b we use 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT} across various system sizes m=2​Lx​Lym=2L_{x}L_{y} as the ground truth against which to benchmark heuristic optimization. We run a simple implementation of local gradient ascent on the Slater manifold from random initializations and record the fraction of starts that reach the global 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT}. This fraction falls sharply as the lattice grows for any fixed number of iteration steps, from near unity at the smallest sizes to near zero at m=64m=64. This gives evidence that a naïve gradient ascent for solving this optimization problem may only be reliable at small system sizes. In contrast, the classical algorithm we propose comes with guarantees and has poly⁡(m)\mathrm{poly}(m) scaling for fixed number of particles and precision.

In Fig. 4c, we capture aspects of the optimization landscape for the closest Slater problem in various ensembles of fermionic states. In particular, we study rank-2 random mixed states, Haar-random pure states, weakly correlated states (comprising superpositions of three to six Slaters with comparable weights), ground states of spinless disordered t−Vt-V chains, and the adversarial states constructed in the proof of Theorem 6. For each state we plot its value of 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT} and the fidelities of spurious stationary points attained as optimization endpoints of randomly initialized simple local gradient ascent. We note that the results shown are representative within each ensemble. Across every ensemble, all spurious stationary points lie strictly below 2/32/3, consistent with Theorem 5 and its mixed-state extension.

The optimization landscapes have several noteworthy features. The spurious stationary points lie well below 2/32/3 for the non-adversarial ensembles: those found are at most ≈0.13,0.19,0.39\approx 0.13,0.19,0.39, and 0.490.49 for mixed, Haar, weakly correlated, and physical. The latter is due to a translation symmetry-broken charge density wave ground state at large repulsive interaction, which at finite sizes results in the ground state assuming the form of an approximate superposition of Slaters (an exact superposition in the absence of disorder), and hence two closely competing closest Slaters. On the whole, we found it rare for t−Vt-V model ground states to exhibit spurious stationary points. This suggests that the optimization landscape for physical states may be benign in general, though more comprehensive study is needed. Meanwhile, the random and weakly correlated state ensembles exhibit rugged landscapes with many spurious stationary points; however, these are less relevant to practical applications and the spurious stationary points concentrate at ≲0.25\lesssim 0.25 at this system size (n=5,m=10n=5,m=10). The adversarial states, by contrast, drive spurious stationary points up to the threshold (0.642≈2/30.642\approx 2/3 at n=16n=16). While confirming Theorem 6, this suggests that 2/32/3 may be a worst case threshold.

VII Discussion

We have studied the task of finding the closest Slater determinant to a given nn-fermion state on mm modes, with closeness measured by fidelity. On the classical side, we have provided an algorithm (Theorem 1) achieving this within ε\varepsilon additive error with time complexity mpoly​(n,1/ε)m^{\text{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon)}. Moreover, Theorem 3 establishes a matching parameterized hardness lower bound under the exponential time hypothesis, so the exponential-in-nn dependence is essentially unavoidable classically. On the quantum side, Theorem 2 provides an algorithm with sample complexity to poly​(m,n,1/ε)\text{poly}(m,n,1/\varepsilon) via the quantum threshold search algorithm of Ref. [6]. In both the classical and quantum settings, we have shown that the time complexity scaling with precision cannot be substantially improved. We have further established that the optimization landscape associated to this problem exhibits an interesting transition at a fidelity of 2/32/3. In particular, Theorem 5 certifies that any locally-optimal Slater with fidelity above 2/32/3 is the globally optimal one.

Our problem is an instance of the broader learning task of agnostic tomography [32, 17] and is adjacent to several other optimization problems. It is similar to the Hartree-Fock approximation, which minimizes the energy of a fermionic Hamiltonian over Slater determinants and is the standard mean-field starting point in chemistry and condensed matter [41, 22], but here a given state ρ\rho is the central object rather than a Hamiltonian. Moreover, a close bosonic analog to our problem is the closest product state learning problem studied by Bakshi et al. [8]. We note that Bakshi et al. focus on a quantum access model obtain more favorable complexities than found here. Moreover, in the special case 𝖮𝖯𝖳=1\mathsf{OPT}=1, when the state is exactly a Slater determinant, the algorithms of Aaronson and Grewal [1], O’Gorman [45], and Christensen and Zhao [18] achieve poly​(m,n,1/ε)\text{poly}(m,n,1/\varepsilon) runtime using the 1-RDM alone, though these algorithms do not generally extend to 𝖮𝖯𝖳<1\mathsf{OPT}<1.

There are several interesting directions for future study. First, it would be interesting to relax particle number conservation and study the problem of learning the closest fermionic Gaussian state [44], which could better accommodate phenomena such as superconductivity; we note, however, that superconducting order can be straightforwardly probed at fixed particle number via off-diagonal long-range order. Second, our quantum protocol attains poly⁡(n,1/ε)\mathrm{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon) sample complexity but retains an exponential-in-nn runtime, and it remains open whether the quantum access model admits a subexponential-time algorithm or, conversely, a runtime lower bound on nn mirroring the classical case. Third, it would be interesting to apply our algorithm at reasonable nn to strongly correlated systems to detect the possibility of “free fermions in disguise”, or unexpectedly high fidelity with the Slater manifold. Finally, a number of natural extensions suggest themselves, such as generalizing to the presence of symmetry-averaged Slater determinants, which may have 𝖮𝖯𝖳≪1\mathsf{OPT}\ll 1 but are still qualitatively Slater-like, or other physically motivated metrics besides fidelity.

Note added.— Upon completing this work, we became aware of independent and concurrent work also addressing the problem of learning the closest Slater determinant [7]. The authors report similar results including a high-fidelity algorithm and a low-fidelity algorithm with a superpolynomial dependence in the number of particles.
