Appendix A Computational hardness

A.1 Classical hardness in nn from parameterized complexity

See 3

Proof of Theorem 3.

We prove this by embedding the nn-Multicolored Clique problem into the problem of learning the closest Slater. Assume we have a graph with color classes V1,…,VnV_{1},\ldots,V_{n}, each of size pp, as in Fig. 5, and we are promised that there is zero or one nn-multicolored clique. Under Assumption 1, there is no randomized algorithm running in time f⁡(n)​po⁡(n)f(n)p^{o(n)} which distinguishes these two cases.

We first augment the graph by adding one extra vertex did_{i} to each color class ViV_{i}. We add edges pairwise between all the did_{i}, but no edges connecting the did_{i} to the original vertices. Hence the did_{i} form a disjoint nn-multicolored clique

D=(d1,…,dn).D=(d_{1},\ldots,d_{n}). (47)

After this augmentation, the graph is promised to contain either only the disjoint clique DD, or the disjoint clique DD together with exactly one other nn-multicolored clique CC. We call this augmented graph GG.

Next, we encode this graph into a fermionic state as follows. We set the particle number to be nn and assign one fermionic mode to each vertex of the graph. Thus the total number of modes is

m=|G|=n⁡(p+1).m=|G|=n(p+1). (48)

Next, let 𝒦⁡(G)\mathcal{K}(G) denote the set of nn-multicolored cliques distinct from DD in the graph, so |𝒦⁡(G)|=0|\mathcal{K}(G)|=0 or 11. Each subgraph A⊂GA\subset G of size |A|=n|A|=n naturally defines an nn-particle Slater determinant, which we will denote |A⟩|A\rangle. Using this convention, we define an unnormalized fermionic state

|ΦG⟩=|D⟩+α​∑C∈𝒦⁡(G)|C⟩,|\Phi_{G}\rangle=|D\rangle+\alpha\sum_{C\in\mathcal{K}(G)}|C\rangle, (49)

where α>1\alpha>1 is chosen so that α21+α2>λ\frac{\alpha^{2}}{1+\alpha^{2}}>\lambda. We depict |ΦG⟩|\Phi_{G}\rangle heuristically in Fig. 6.

Next, we establish that |ΦG⟩|\Phi_{G}\rangle indeed has a succinct classical description. To see this, we fix any set I⊂[m]I\subset[m] of size |I|=n|I|=n and note that

⟨I|ΦG⟩={1,I=D,α,I∈𝒦⁡(G),0,otherwise,\langle I|\Phi_{G}\rangle=\begin{cases}1,&I=D,\\ \alpha,&I\in\mathcal{K}(G),\\ 0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (50)

which is efficient to compute. Indeed, checking I=DI=D is trivial while checking I∈𝒦⁡(G)I\in\mathcal{K}(G) is an O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) operation. We note that the norm of the state ‖ΦG‖\|\Phi_{G}\| is by necessity unknown to the succinct description, as computing it would involve a sum over all exponentially many I⊂[m]I\subset[m].

Under our assumptions on the graph, we have two possibilities:

|ΦG⟩={|D⟩|𝒦⁡(G)|=0|D⟩+α​|C⟩|𝒦⁡(G)|=1,|\Phi_{G}\rangle=\begin{cases}|D\rangle&|\mathcal{K}(G)|=0\\ |D\rangle+\alpha|C\rangle&|\mathcal{K}(G)|=1,\end{cases} (51)

where CC is the unique nn-multicolored clique distinct from DD. Since DD and CC have orthogonal one-particle subspaces, by Lemma 6, we have

𝖮𝖯𝖳={1,|𝒦⁡(G)|=0,α2/(1+α2),|𝒦⁡(G)|=1.\mathsf{OPT}=\begin{cases}1,&|\mathcal{K}(G)|=0,\\ \alpha^{2}/(1+\alpha^{2}),&|\mathcal{K}(G)|=1.\end{cases} (52)

Moreover, the optimum is attained uniquely, up to phase, by |D⟩|D\rangle in the first case and by |C⟩|C\rangle in the second case. By our choice of α\alpha, the promise 𝖮𝖯𝖳≥λ\mathsf{OPT}\geq\lambda holds in both cases.

At this point, we choose a constant ελ\varepsilon_{\lambda} as follows:

ελ=min⁡{716,α2−(α−(α−1)/4)21+α2}.\varepsilon_{\lambda}=\min\left\{\frac{7}{16},\frac{\alpha^{2}-(\alpha-(\alpha-1)/4)^{2}}{1+\alpha^{2}}\right\}. (53)

This depends implicitly on λ\lambda since the choice of α\alpha depended on λ\lambda. The reason for this particular choice will be evident in the next steps.

Now suppose, for contradiction, we have a randomized algorithm that outputs a Slater determinant |S⟩|S\rangle which satisfies Eq. (29), running in time f⁡(n)​mo⁡(n)f(n)m^{o(n)} with success probability at least 0.990.99. We will show that this algorithm can distinguish |𝒦⁡(G)|=0,1|\mathcal{K}(G)|=0,1, contradicting Assumption 1.

In the case |𝒦⁡(G)|=0|\mathcal{K}(G)|=0, we have |ΦG⟩=|D⟩|\Phi_{G}\rangle=|D\rangle and 𝖮𝖯𝖳=1\mathsf{OPT}=1, and hence

|⟨S|D⟩|2≥1−ελ.|\langle S|D\rangle|^{2}\geq 1-\varepsilon_{\lambda}. (54)

In particular, since ελ≤7/16\varepsilon_{\lambda}\leq 7/16, we have |⟨S|D⟩|>3/4.|\langle S|D\rangle|>3/4.

In the case |𝒦⁡(G)|=1|\mathcal{K}(G)|=1, by Lemma 6 we have

|⟨S|D⟩|+|⟨S|C⟩|≤1.|\langle S|D\rangle|+|\langle S|C\rangle|\leq 1. (55)

Writing x=|⟨S|D⟩|x=|\langle S|D\rangle| for convenience, we have |⟨S|C⟩|≤1−x|\langle S|C\rangle|\leq 1-x and therefore

|⟨S|ΦG⟩|‖ΦG‖\displaystyle\frac{|\langle S|\Phi_{G}\rangle|}{\|\Phi_{G}\|} ≤x+α⁡(1−x)1+α2=α−(α−1)​x1+α2\displaystyle\leq\frac{x+\alpha(1-x)}{\sqrt{1+\alpha^{2}}}=\frac{\alpha-(\alpha-1)x}{\sqrt{1+\alpha^{2}}} (56)

since |D⟩|D\rangle and |C⟩|C\rangle have disjoint occupied subspaces. If x≥1/4x\geq 1/4, then

|⟨S|ΦG⟩|2‖ΦG‖2≤(α−(α−1)/4)21+α2.\frac{|\langle S|\Phi_{G}\rangle|^{2}}{\|\Phi_{G}\|^{2}}\leq\frac{(\alpha-(\alpha-1)/4)^{2}}{1+\alpha^{2}}. (57)

Since α>1\alpha>1, this is strictly smaller than the optimum value 𝖮𝖯𝖳=α21+α2.\mathsf{OPT}=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{1+\alpha^{2}}. Define the quantity

Δα≔α2−(α−(α−1)/4)21+α2>0.\Delta_{\alpha}\coloneqq\frac{\alpha^{2}-(\alpha-(\alpha-1)/4)^{2}}{1+\alpha^{2}}>0. (58)

Thus, in the case |𝒦⁡(G)|=1|\mathcal{K}(G)|=1, if |⟨S|D⟩|≥1/4|\langle S|D\rangle|\geq 1/4 then |S⟩|S\rangle is at least Δα\Delta_{\alpha} below optimal. Equivalently, if |S⟩|S\rangle is within Δα\Delta_{\alpha} of being optimal, then |⟨S|D⟩|<1/4|\langle S|D\rangle|<1/4. Since ελ≤Δα\varepsilon_{\lambda}\leq\Delta_{\alpha}, if |S⟩|S\rangle is within ελ\varepsilon_{\lambda} of being optimal, then |⟨S|D⟩|<1/4|\langle S|D\rangle|<1/4.

Finally, we use this to distinguish the two cases as follows. Given the augmented graph GG and succinct classical description for |ΦG⟩|\Phi_{G}\rangle, we run the hypothetical closest-Slater algorithm and obtain |S⟩|S\rangle. Since D⊂GD\subset G is explicitly known by construction, we can compute |⟨S|D⟩||\langle S|D\rangle| efficiently to constant precision and declare “no clique” if |⟨S|D⟩|>1/2|\langle S|D\rangle|>1/2 and “yes clique” otherwise. By the preceding arguments, this distinguishes the two possible cases. The total runtime is

f⁡(n)​(n⁡(p+1))o⁡(n)=f′​(n)​po⁡(n),f(n)\bigl(n(p+1)\bigr)^{o(n)}=f^{\prime}(n)p^{o(n)}, (59)

contradicting Assumption 1. Hence no such algorithm exists, completing the proof. ∎

A.2 Hardness in precision from the quantum separability problem

The quantum learning algorithm described in Theorem 2 brings the sample complexity down to poly⁡(m,n,1/ε)\mathrm{poly}(m,n,1/\varepsilon), but its runtime remains exponential. In this section, we show that this inefficiency is inevitable, by proving that no quantum algorithm can solve the problem to ε=1/poly⁡(m)\varepsilon=1/\mathrm{poly}(m) accuracy in poly⁡(m)\mathrm{poly}(m) time even when there are only n=2n=2 fermions, unless 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP} is in 𝖡𝖰𝖯\mathsf{BQP}. This holds true even if the algorithm is given the complete classical description of the input state ρ\rho, and hence the hardness result also applies to the quantum copy access model since poly⁡(m)\mathrm{poly}(m)-dimensional quantum states can be prepared in poly⁡(m)\mathrm{poly}(m) time from their classical descriptions.

See 4

We prove Theorem 4 by reducing the task of finding the Slater determinant closest to a two-fermion state to the task of finding the product state closest to a bipartite state, also known as the quantum separability problem [33, 26]. Ref. [26] proved that solving the quantum separability problem to inverse-polynomial accuracy is 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-hard, and hence our hardness result follows.

The intuition behind the reduction can be understood as follows. Consider two fermions in an even number of mm modes. One can interpret these modes as d=m/2d=m/2 spatial modes and a spin-1/21/2 degree of freedom. For a Slater determinant in which the two fermions have opposite spins, the anti-symmetry requirement can always be satisfied by anti-symmetrizing the spin degree of freedom, and leaving the spatial wavefunction in an ordinary product state. Hence, finding the closest Slater determinant is the same as finding the closest product state in the opposite-spin sector, where the spin label marks the bipartition, provided that Slater determinants built from wavefunctions that mix the two spin sectors cannot outperform opposite-spin ones. We formalize this idea and prove Theorem 4 in the following.

Proof of Theorem 4.

We begin by invoking the computational hardness of the quantum separability problem.

Lemma 1 (Computational hardness of quantum separability, [26]).

There exists a constant c0>0c_{0}>0 such that the following promise problem is 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-hard: given M∈ℂd2×d2,0⪯M⪯I,M≠0,γ∈[0,1]M\in\mathbb{C}^{d^{2}\times d^{2}},0\preceq M\preceq I,M\neq 0,\gamma\in[0,1], decide whether

max|x⟩,|y⟩∈ℂd⟨x|x⟩=⟨y|y⟩=1⁡(⟨x|⊗⟨y|)​M​(|x⟩⊗|y⟩)≥γ+1/dc0\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}|x\rangle,|y\rangle\in\mathbb{C}^{d}\\ \langle x|x\rangle=\langle y|y\rangle=1\end{subarray}}(\langle x|\otimes\langle y|)M(|x\rangle\otimes|y\rangle)\geq\gamma+1/d^{c_{0}} (60)

or

max|x⟩,|y⟩∈ℂd⟨x|x⟩=⟨y|y⟩=1⁡(⟨x|⊗⟨y|)​M​(|x⟩⊗|y⟩)≤γ−1/dc0.\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}|x\rangle,|y\rangle\in\mathbb{C}^{d}\\ \langle x|x\rangle=\langle y|y\rangle=1\end{subarray}}(\langle x|\otimes\langle y|)M(|x\rangle\otimes|y\rangle)\leq\gamma-1/d^{c_{0}}. (61)

For simplicity, we define

hSep​(M)=max|x⟩,|y⟩∈ℂd⟨x|x⟩=⟨y|y⟩=1⁡(⟨x|⊗⟨y|)​M​(|x⟩⊗|y⟩).h_{\mathrm{Sep}}(M)=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}|x\rangle,|y\rangle\in\mathbb{C}^{d}\\ \langle x|x\rangle=\langle y|y\rangle=1\end{subarray}}(\langle x|\otimes\langle y|)M(|x\rangle\otimes|y\rangle). (62)

Without loss of generality, we assume that mm is even and let d=m/2d=m/2. We label the single fermion Hilbert space as ℋ1=ℂd⊗ℂ2\mathcal{H}_{1}=\mathbb{C}^{d}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{2} and use |xσ⟩=|x⟩⊗|σ⟩,|x⟩∈ℂd,σ∈{↑,↓}|x^{\sigma}\rangle=|x\rangle\otimes|\sigma\rangle,|x\rangle\in\mathbb{C}^{d},\sigma\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\} to denote the state vectors. Let |ei⟩,i=1,…,d|e_{i}\rangle,i=1,\ldots,d be the standard basis of ℂd\mathbb{C}^{d}. Then the opposite-spin sector is the span of {|ei↑⟩∧|ej↓⟩}i,j=1d\{|e_{i}^{\uparrow}\rangle\wedge|e_{j}^{\downarrow}\rangle\}_{i,j=1}^{d}. These d2d^{2} vectors are orthonormal and hence the map

J:ℂd⊗ℂd→ℋ2=∧2(ℂd⊗ℂ2),J:\mathbb{C}^{d}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{d}\to\mathcal{H}_{2}=\wedge^{2}(\mathbb{C}^{d}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{2}), (63)

satisfying

J⁡(|ei⟩⊗|ej⟩)=|ei↑⟩∧|ej↓⟩,J(|e_{i}\rangle\otimes|e_{j}\rangle)=|e_{i}^{\uparrow}\rangle\wedge|e_{j}^{\downarrow}\rangle, (64)

is an isometry from the bipartite d×dd\times d dimension Hilbert space to the opposite-spin sector (Fig. 7). Since JJ is linear, we have J⁡(|x⟩⊗|y⟩)=|x↑⟩∧|y↓⟩J(|x\rangle\otimes|y\rangle)=|x^{\uparrow}\rangle\wedge|y^{\downarrow}\rangle. Moreover, |x↑⟩|x^{\uparrow}\rangle and |y↓⟩|y^{\downarrow}\rangle are orthonormal whenever |x⟩|x\rangle and |y⟩|y\rangle are unit vectors, because the spin degree of freedom guarantees orthogonality. Hence, JJ maps product states to Slater determinants.

Now, we use the matrix MM from Lemma 1 to construct a two-fermion state

ρM=J​M​J†Tr⁡(M).\rho_{M}=\frac{JMJ^{\dagger}}{\Tr(M)}. (65)

This is a valid (2​d2)\binom{2d}{2}-dimensional density matrix, because 0⪯M⪯I0\preceq M\preceq I and JJ is an isometry. By construction, the Slater fidelity satisfies

F⁡(|x↑⟩∧|y↓⟩)=1Tr⁡(M)​(⟨x|⊗⟨y|)​M​(|x⟩⊗|y⟩).\mathrm{F}(|x^{\uparrow}\rangle\wedge|y^{\downarrow}\rangle)=\frac{1}{\Tr(M)}(\langle x|\otimes\langle y|)M(|x\rangle\otimes|y\rangle). (66)

Therefore, we already have

𝖮𝖯𝖳=maxS⁡F⁡(|S⟩)≥maxx,y⁡F⁡(|x↑⟩∧|y↓⟩)=hSep​(M)Tr⁡(M).\mathsf{OPT}=\max_{S}\mathrm{F}(|S\rangle)\geq\max_{x,y}\mathrm{F}(|x^{\uparrow}\rangle\wedge|y^{\downarrow}\rangle)=\frac{h_{\mathrm{Sep}}(M)}{\Tr(M)}. (67)

Next, we prove that 𝖮𝖯𝖳≤hSep​(M)Tr⁡(M)\mathsf{OPT}\leq\frac{h_{\mathrm{Sep}}(M)}{\Tr(M)} to establish their equality: 𝖮𝖯𝖳=hSep​(M)Tr⁡(M)\mathsf{OPT}=\frac{h_{\mathrm{Sep}}(M)}{\Tr(M)}. To this end, note that any two-fermion Slater determinant can be written as |T⟩=|w1⟩∧|w2⟩|T\rangle=|w_{1}\rangle\wedge|w_{2}\rangle, where |w1⟩,|w2⟩|w_{1}\rangle,|w_{2}\rangle are orthonormal. Furthermore, every single particle state vector |wk⟩,k=1,2|w_{k}\rangle,k=1,2 can be decomposed into spin-up and spin-down parts

|wk⟩=|ak↑⟩+|bk↓⟩,|w_{k}\rangle=|a_{k}^{\uparrow}\rangle+|b_{k}^{\downarrow}\rangle, (68)

where ‖|ak⟩‖2+‖|bk⟩‖2=1,|ak⟩,|bk⟩∈ℂd\||a_{k}\rangle\|^{2}+\||b_{k}\rangle\|^{2}=1,|a_{k}\rangle,|b_{k}\rangle\in\mathbb{C}^{d} are the unnormalized spatial wavefunctions. From the linearity of the wedge product, we have

|T⟩=|a1↑⟩∧|a2↑⟩+|b1↓⟩∧|b2↓⟩+|a1↑⟩∧|b2↓⟩+|b1↓⟩∧|a2↑⟩.\begin{split}|T\rangle=&|a_{1}^{\uparrow}\rangle\wedge|a_{2}^{\uparrow}\rangle+|b_{1}^{\downarrow}\rangle\wedge|b_{2}^{\downarrow}\rangle\\ &+|a_{1}^{\uparrow}\rangle\wedge|b_{2}^{\downarrow}\rangle+|b_{1}^{\downarrow}\rangle\wedge|a_{2}^{\uparrow}\rangle.\end{split} (69)

Note that only the last two terms are in the opposite-spin sector, and hence the preimage of |T⟩|T\rangle under the map JJ reads

J†​|T⟩=J†​(|a1↑⟩∧|b2↓⟩−|a2↑⟩∧|b1↓⟩)=|a1⟩⊗|b2⟩−|a2⟩⊗|b1⟩=|ϕT⟩,\begin{split}J^{\dagger}|T\rangle&=J^{\dagger}(|a_{1}^{\uparrow}\rangle\wedge|b_{2}^{\downarrow}\rangle-|a_{2}^{\uparrow}\rangle\wedge|b_{1}^{\downarrow}\rangle)\\ &=|a_{1}\rangle\otimes|b_{2}\rangle-|a_{2}\rangle\otimes|b_{1}\rangle\\ &=|\phi_{T}\rangle,\end{split} (70)

where we have used the anti-symmetry of wedge product and defined |ϕT⟩=|a1⟩⊗|b2⟩−|a2⟩⊗|b1⟩|\phi_{T}\rangle=|a_{1}\rangle\otimes|b_{2}\rangle-|a_{2}\rangle\otimes|b_{1}\rangle. Hence, we have

F⁡(|T⟩)=1Tr⁡(M)​⟨ϕT|M|ϕT⟩\mathrm{F}(|T\rangle)=\frac{1}{\Tr(M)}\langle\phi_{T}|M|\phi_{T}\rangle (71)

for any Slater determinant |T⟩|T\rangle. Note that

⟨ϕT|M|ϕT⟩=‖M1/2​|ϕT⟩‖2≤(‖M1/2​|a1⟩⊗|b2⟩‖+‖M1/2​|a2⟩⊗|b1⟩‖)2,\begin{split}&\langle\phi_{T}|M|\phi_{T}\rangle=\|M^{1/2}|\phi_{T}\rangle\|^{2}\\ &\leq(\|M^{1/2}|a_{1}\rangle\otimes|b_{2}\rangle\|+\|M^{1/2}|a_{2}\rangle\otimes|b_{1}\rangle\|)^{2},\end{split} (72)

via triangle inequality. Also for any unnormalized vectors |a⟩,|b⟩∈ℂd|a\rangle,|b\rangle\in\mathbb{C}^{d}, we have

‖M1/2​|a⟩⊗|b⟩‖2≤‖|a⟩‖2​‖|b⟩‖2​hSep​(M).\|M^{1/2}|a\rangle\otimes|b\rangle\|^{2}\leq\||a\rangle\|^{2}\||b\rangle\|^{2}h_{\mathrm{Sep}}(M). (73)

Therefore, we have

⟨ϕT|M|ϕT⟩≤hSep​(M)​(‖|a1⟩‖​‖|b2⟩‖+‖|a2⟩‖​‖|b1⟩‖)2.\langle\phi_{T}|M|\phi_{T}\rangle\leq h_{\mathrm{Sep}}(M)(\||a_{1}\rangle\|\||b_{2}\rangle\|+\||a_{2}\rangle\|\||b_{1}\rangle\|)^{2}. (74)

Using the normalization condition ∥|ak⟩∥2+∥|bk⟩∥2=1,k=1,2\||a_{k}\rangle\|^{2}+\||b_{k}\rangle\|^{2}=1,k=1,2, we may parameterize the norms as ‖|ak⟩‖=cos⁡(θk),‖|bk⟩‖=sin⁡(θk)\||a_{k}\rangle\|=\cos(\theta_{k}),\||b_{k}\rangle\|=\sin(\theta_{k}). This means that

‖|a1⟩‖​‖|b2⟩‖+‖|a2⟩‖​‖|b1⟩‖=cosθ1sinθ2+cosθ2sinθ1=sin⁡(θ1+θ2)∈[0,1].\begin{split}\||a_{1}\rangle\|\||b_{2}\rangle\|+\||a_{2}\rangle\|\||b_{1}\rangle\|&=\cos\theta_{1}\sin\theta_{2}+\cos\theta_{2}\sin\theta_{1}\\ &=\sin(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2})\in[0,1].\end{split} (75)

Hence, we have

F⁡(|T⟩)≤hSep​(M)Tr⁡(M)\mathrm{F}(|T\rangle)\leq\frac{h_{\mathrm{Sep}}(M)}{\Tr(M)} (76)

for any Slater determinant |T⟩|T\rangle and therefore

𝖮𝖯𝖳≤hSep​(M)Tr⁡(M).\mathsf{OPT}\leq\frac{h_{\mathrm{Sep}}(M)}{\Tr(M)}. (77)

Combined with the other direction, we have

𝖮𝖯𝖳=hSep​(M)Tr⁡(M)\mathsf{OPT}=\frac{h_{\mathrm{Sep}}(M)}{\Tr(M)} (78)

Now we are finally ready to prove the computational hardness. For the sake of contradiction, assume that there is a polynomial-time quantum algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} that takes as input the classical description of any density matrix ρ\rho of n=2n=2 fermions on mm modes and outputs a Slater determinant |S⟩|S\rangle satisfying

⟨S|ρ|S⟩≥𝖮𝖯𝖳−1/mc\langle S|\rho|S\rangle\geq\mathsf{OPT}-1/m^{c} (79)

with probability at least 2/32/3. In the following, we design a polynomial-time quantum algorithm that solves the quantum separability problem defined in Lemma 1.

Concretely, given a problem instance (M∈ℂd2×d2,γ)(M\in\mathbb{C}^{d^{2}\times d^{2}},\gamma) with problem size dd from the quantum separability problem, we set m=2​dm=2d and first compute the matrix

ρM=J​M​J†Tr⁡(M).\rho_{M}=\frac{JMJ^{\dagger}}{\Tr(M)}. (80)

This step is a poly⁡(d)=poly⁡(m)\mathrm{poly}(d)=\mathrm{poly}(m) dimensional matrix computation that takes poly⁡(m)\mathrm{poly}(m) time. Next, we run the algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} with ρM\rho_{M} as the input, obtaining an output Slater determinant |T⟩|T\rangle. We orthogonalize and normalize it to obtain the spatial wavefunctions |a1⟩,|b1⟩,|a2⟩,|b2⟩|a_{1}\rangle,|b_{1}\rangle,|a_{2}\rangle,|b_{2}\rangle and calculate the preimage |ϕT⟩=|a1⟩⊗|b2⟩−|a2⟩⊗|b1⟩|\phi_{T}\rangle=|a_{1}\rangle\otimes|b_{2}\rangle-|a_{2}\rangle\otimes|b_{1}\rangle. This step is standard matrix computation and only takes poly⁡(d)=poly⁡(m)\mathrm{poly}(d)=\mathrm{poly}(m) time. Then we calculate the value

v=⟨ϕT|M|ϕT⟩Tr⁡(M)=F⁡(|T⟩).v=\frac{\langle\phi_{T}|M|\phi_{T}\rangle}{\Tr(M)}=\mathrm{F}(|T\rangle). (81)

We always have v≤𝖮𝖯𝖳v\leq\mathsf{OPT} and the guarantee of the learning algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} implies that

𝖮𝖯𝖳−1/mc≤v≤𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT}-1/m^{c}\leq v\leq\mathsf{OPT} (82)

with probability at least 2/32/3. Since 𝖮𝖯𝖳=hSep​(M)Tr⁡(M)\mathsf{OPT}=\frac{h_{\mathrm{Sep}}(M)}{\Tr(M)}, we have that

hSep​(M)−Tr⁡(M)/mc≤Tr⁡(M)​v≤hSep​(M).h_{\mathrm{Sep}}(M)-\Tr(M)/m^{c}\leq\Tr(M)v\leq h_{\mathrm{Sep}}(M). (83)

Moreover, 0⪯M⪯I0\preceq M\preceq I implies that Tr⁡(M)∈[0,d2]\Tr(M)\in[0,d^{2}]. Therefore, we choose c=c0+2c=c_{0}+2 and obtain

hSep​(M)−1/(4​dc0)≤Tr⁡(M)​v≤hSep​(M).h_{\mathrm{Sep}}(M)-1/(4d^{c_{0}})\leq\Tr(M)v\leq h_{\mathrm{Sep}}(M). (84)

Finally, we calculate and compare the value of Tr⁡(M)​v\Tr(M)v against γ\gamma, thus solving the quantum separability problem, which is 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP} hard in d=m/2d=m/2 from Lemma 1. The reduction is completely classical and runs in polynomial time. Hence the existence of a quantum (or classical) learning algorithm that solves the Slater learning problem in poly⁡(m)\mathrm{poly}(m) time implies that 𝖭𝖯⊆𝖡𝖰𝖯\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{BQP} (or 𝖭𝖯⊆𝖡𝖯𝖯\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{BPP}), completing the proof of Theorem 4. ∎

Appendix B Extension to mixed states

In this appendix, we extend the results of the main text to mixed states. Throughout, ρ\rho denotes an arbitrary density matrix on the nn-particle fermionic Hilbert space ℋn\mathcal{H}_{n}, F⁡(S)=⟨S|ρ|S⟩\mathrm{F}(S)=\langle S|\rho|S\rangle, and 𝖮𝖯𝖳=max|S⟩∈𝒮⁡⟨S|ρ|S⟩\mathsf{OPT}=\max_{|S\rangle\in\mathcal{S}}\langle S|\rho|S\rangle. We first specify the access model we assume for the case of ρ\rho a mixed state. We then verify that the algorithmic upper and hardness lower bounds carry over. Finally, we prove the mixed-state analog of the F=2/3\mathrm{F}=2/3 threshold.

In the quantum access model, no modification is needed for an extension to mixed states, as we made no requirement that ρ\rho is pure. In the classical case, we assume the following.

Definition 1 (Succinct classical access to a mixed state).

A succinct classical description of ρ\rho provides, in efficient time per sample, (i) for any few-body observable AA, a sample of a random variable XAX_{A} with 𝔼⁡[XA]=Tr⁡(A​ρ)\mathbb{E}[X_{A}]=\Tr(A\rho) and Var⁡[XA]=O⁡(1)\mathrm{Var}[X_{A}]=O(1), and (ii) for any explicitly specified Slater |S⟩|S\rangle, a sample of a random variable YS∈[0,1]Y_{S}\in[0,1] with 𝔼⁡[YS]=⟨S|ρ|S⟩\mathbb{E}[Y_{S}]=\langle S|\rho|S\rangle.

This directly generalizes the pure-state access model of the main text. It is realized, for instance, by an ensemble representation ρ=∑kpk​|ψk⟩​⟨ψk|\rho=\sum_{k}p_{k}|\psi_{k}\rangle\!\langle\psi_{k}| in which one can sample k∼pk\sim p and each member |ψk⟩|\psi_{k}\rangle is provided with a pure-state succinct description. We can now state the following algorithms for the mixed state case.

Proposition 1 (Algorithmic results for mixed states).

Let ρ\rho be an arbitrary mixed nn-fermion state. Under Definition 1, the classical algorithm of Theorem 1 returns a Slater determinant with fidelity at least 𝖮𝖯𝖳−ε\mathsf{OPT}-\varepsilon, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, in time exp⁡[O⁡(n3ε​log⁡nε)]⋅poly⁡(m,log⁡1δ)\exp\left[O\left(\frac{n^{3}}{\varepsilon}\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon}\right)\right]\cdot\mathrm{poly}(m,\log\frac{1}{\delta}). Given quantum copies of ρ\rho, the protocol of Theorem 2 applies verbatim with the same sample complexity.

Proof.

Let us verify that each step of the proof of Theorem 1 applies for a general density matrix. First, we note that Lemmas 4 and 5 are stated and proven for an arbitrary density matrix ρ\rho, with γi​j=Tr⁡(cj†​ci​ρ)\gamma_{ij}=\Tr(c_{j}^{\dagger}c_{i}\rho) and tr⁡γ=n\operatorname{tr}\gamma=n, so the construction of the active space 𝒜\mathcal{A} with dim𝒜=O⁡(n2/ε)\dim\mathcal{A}=O(n^{2}/\varepsilon) and the bound 𝖮𝖯𝖳≤𝖮𝖯𝖳𝒜+ε/2\mathsf{OPT}\leq\mathsf{OPT}_{\mathcal{A}}+\varepsilon/2 require no change. Second, in Theorem 1, |F⁡(U)−F⁡(V)|≤2​n​‖U−V‖F|\mathrm{F}(U)-\mathrm{F}(V)|\leq 2n\|U-V\|_{F} needs only that ‖ρ‖≤1\|\rho\|\leq 1, which holds for a general ρ\rho. Hence the covering net constructed with size M=exp⁡[O⁡(n3ε​log⁡nε)]M=\exp\left[O\left(\frac{n^{3}}{\varepsilon}\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon}\right)\right] remains unchanged. Third, the exact evaluation of fidelities which was assumed in Theorem 1 is replaced by estimation under Definition 1. It suffices to straightforwardly estimate ⟨Sk|ρ|Sk⟩\langle S_{k}|\rho|S_{k}\rangle for each net point to additive error ε/8\varepsilon/8 with failure probability δ/M\delta/M, which by Hoeffding’s inequality costs O⁡(ε−2​log⁡(M/δ))O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(M/\delta)) samples per point. A union bound gives a total failure probability δ\delta, and returning the empirical maximum over the net costs at most an additional ε/4\varepsilon/4 by our choice of covering net. By ε/8+ε/4<ε/2\varepsilon/8+\varepsilon/4<\varepsilon/2, we can then apply the conclusion of Theorem 1.

For the quantum protocol, we may note that the threshold search and Lemma 9 are formulated for an arbitrary state ρ\rho through the quantities Tr⁡(ρ​Ai)\Tr(\rho A_{i}), and the fermionic classical shadow estimation of γ\gamma in Lemma 5 makes no assumption on purity. Hence Theorem 2 applies verbatim. ∎

Next, we remark that since pure states are a subset of mixed states, and the pure-state succinct classical description used by Theorem 3 fits under our mixed-state access model if we allow generalization to unnormalized ρ\rho, and hence the computational hardness lower bounds transfer. In particular, the parameterized hardness lower bound of Theorem 3 applies to the mixed-state problem without modification and the proof of the sharpness of the 2/3 threshold in Theorem 6 extends for the same reason. Moreover, we may note that the NP-hardness result of Theorem 4 is already stated for mixed states. Indeed, the hard instances of this theorem are mixed states.

Next, we turn to the high-fidelity regime and the F=2/3\mathrm{F}=2/3 threshold. Recall that Theorem 5 showed the following: for a pure state |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle and Slater |G⟩|G\rangle, if |⟨G|ψ⟩|2>2/3|\langle G|\psi\rangle|^{2}>2/3 and a local stationarity condition BG=0B_{G}=0 holds, then |G⟩|G\rangle is globally closest. Following a similar approach, let us fix a Slater |G⟩|G\rangle with occupied orbitals gμg_{\mu} and unoccupied orbitals faf_{a}, and let Π1G\Pi_{1}^{G} denote the projector onto the span of the single particle-hole excitations |Ga​μ⟩=cfa†​cgμ​|G⟩|G_{a\mu}\rangle=c_{f_{a}}^{\dagger}c_{g_{\mu}}|G\rangle. We define the mixed residual

RG≔‖Π1G​ρ​|G⟩‖=∑a​μ|⟨Ga​μ|ρ|G⟩|2.R_{G}\coloneqq\|\Pi_{1}^{G}\rho|G\rangle\|=\sqrt{\sum_{a\mu}|\langle G_{a\mu}|\rho|G\rangle|^{2}}. (85)

The following Lemma generalizes Lemma 7 and identifies RG=0R_{G}=0 as the correct Brillouin condition for mixed states.

Lemma 2 (Mixed state Brillouin condition).

The first variation of F⁡(G)=⟨G|ρ|G⟩\mathrm{F}(G)=\langle G|\rho|G\rangle over the manifold of Slater determinants vanishes at |G⟩|G\rangle if and only if RG=0R_{G}=0.

Proof.

By Lemma 7, the tangent space at |G⟩|G\rangle is spanned by the excitations |Ga​μ⟩|G_{a\mu}\rangle (and trivially i​|G⟩i|G\rangle) so that a path on the manifold passing through |G⟩|G\rangle at τ=0\tau=0 takes the form |G⁡(τ)⟩=|G⟩+τ​∑a​μTa​μ​|Ga​μ⟩+O⁡(τ2)|G(\tau)\rangle=|G\rangle+\tau\sum_{a\mu}T_{a\mu}|G_{a\mu}\rangle+O(\tau^{2}) up to phase. Substituting, we have

⟨G⁡(τ)|ρ|G⁡(τ)⟩=⟨G​|ρ⁡|G⟩+2​τ​Re​∑a​μTa​μ¯​⟨Ga​μ|​ρ|​G⟩+O⁡(τ2).\langle G(\tau)|\rho|G(\tau)\rangle=\langle G|\rho|G\rangle+2\tau\mathrm{Re}\sum_{a\mu}\overline{T_{a\mu}}\langle G_{a\mu}|\rho|G\rangle+O(\tau^{2}). (86)

The linear term must vanish for arbitrary coefficients Ta​μT_{a\mu} in order for the first variation with respect to τ\tau to vanish. This holds if and only if ⟨Ga​μ|ρ|G⟩=0\langle G_{a\mu}|\rho|G\rangle=0 for all a,μa,\mu. ∎

We also point out that Lemma 8 (the technical result bounding higher-particle hole excitations using an inequality q≤2​(1−s)q\leq\sqrt{2}(1-s)) makes no reference to ρ\rho and hence applies here unchanged. An important next step will be a decomposition of ρ\rho into a pure state plus a remainder σ\sigma, formalized below.

Lemma 3 (Mixed state decomposition).

Let ρ⪰0\rho\succeq 0 and let |G⟩|G\rangle be a unit vector with α=⟨G|ρ|G⟩>0\alpha=\langle G|\rho|G\rangle>0. Define |ϕ⟩≔ρ​|G⟩/α|\phi\rangle\coloneqq\rho|G\rangle/\sqrt{\alpha}. Then

ρ=|ϕ⟩​⟨ϕ|+σ\rho=|\phi\rangle\!\langle\phi|+\sigma (87)

with σ⪰0\sigma\succeq 0 and σ​|G⟩=0\sigma|G\rangle=0.

Proof.

For any vector |x⟩|x\rangle, Cauchy-Schwarz applied to the positive semidefinite bilinear form ρ\rho gives us |⟨x|ρ|G⟩|2≤⟨x|ρ⁡|x⟩​⟨G|​ρ|G⟩|\langle x|\rho|G\rangle|^{2}\leq\langle x|\rho|x\rangle\langle G|\rho|G\rangle, which is equivalent to |⟨x|ϕ⟩|2≤⟨x|ρ|x⟩|\langle x|\phi\rangle|^{2}\leq\langle x|\rho|x\rangle and proves that σ=ρ−|ϕ⟩​⟨ϕ|⪰0\sigma=\rho-|\phi\rangle\!\langle\phi|\succeq 0. By definition of |ϕ⟩|\phi\rangle we have ⟨ϕ|G⟩=α\langle\phi|G\rangle=\sqrt{\alpha}, and hence σ⁡|G⟩=ρ⁡|G⟩−α​|ϕ⟩=0\sigma|G\rangle=\rho|G\rangle-\sqrt{\alpha}|\phi\rangle=0. ∎

We are now in a position to establish the F=2/3\mathrm{F}=2/3 threshold for mixed states.

Theorem 7 (2/32/3 certificate for mixed states).

Let ρ\rho be an nn-fermion density matrix on ℋn\mathcal{H}_{n} and let |G⟩|G\rangle be a Slater determinant such that α=⟨G|ρ|G⟩≥2/3\alpha=\langle G|\rho|G\rangle\geq 2/3. Then every Slater determinant |H⟩|H\rangle satisfies

⟨H|ρ|H⟩≤α−(3​α2−1)​(1−|⟨G|H⟩|2)+2​RG​1−|⟨G|H⟩|2\langle H|\rho|H\rangle\leq\alpha-\left(\frac{3\alpha}{2}-1\right)\left(1-|\langle G|H\rangle|^{2}\right)\\ +2R_{G}\sqrt{1-|\langle G|H\rangle|^{2}} (88)

with RGR_{G} defined in Eq. (85). In particular, if α>2/3\alpha>2/3 and RG=0R_{G}=0, then |G⟩|G\rangle is the unique globally closest Slater to ρ\rho, up to phase. Moreover, if α≥2/3+Δ\alpha\geq 2/3+\Delta for some Δ>0\Delta>0, then

𝖮𝖯𝖳≤α+23​RG2Δ.\mathsf{OPT}\leq\alpha+\frac{2}{3}\frac{R_{G}^{2}}{\Delta}. (89)
Proof.

Let |H⟩|H\rangle be an arbitrary Slater and decompose it into particle-hole sectors relative to |G⟩|G\rangle,

|H⟩=s⁡|G⟩+|h1⟩+|h≥2⟩,|H\rangle=s|G\rangle+|h_{1}\rangle+|h_{\geq 2}\rangle, (90)

with overall phase chosen so that s=|⟨G|H⟩|s=|\langle G|H\rangle|. We set p=‖|h1⟩‖2p=\||h_{1}\rangle\|^{2} and q=‖|h≥2⟩‖q=\||h_{\geq 2}\rangle\| so that s2+p+q2=1s^{2}+p+q^{2}=1, and Lemma 8 then gives q≤2​(1−s)q\leq\sqrt{2}(1-s). Using Lemma 3, we write

⟨H|ρ|H⟩=|⟨H|ϕ⟩|2+⟨H​|σ|​H⟩,\langle H|\rho|H\rangle=|\langle H|\phi\rangle|^{2}+\langle H|\sigma|H\rangle, (91)

and we bound the two terms separately. Using the notation of Lemma 3, we decompose |ϕ⟩|\phi\rangle as

|ϕ⟩=α​|G⟩+|ϕ1⟩+|ϕ≥2⟩|\phi\rangle=\sqrt{\alpha}|G\rangle+|\phi_{1}\rangle+|\phi_{\geq 2}\rangle (92)

with ‖|ϕ1⟩‖=RG/α\||\phi_{1}\rangle\|=R_{G}/\sqrt{\alpha}. We also write w=‖|ϕ≥2⟩‖w=\||\phi_{\geq 2}\rangle\| and T=Tr⁡σT=\Tr\sigma. Due to the proliferation of variables, we relist some definitions:

α\displaystyle\alpha =⟨G|ρ|G⟩,|ϕ⟩=ρ|G⟩/α|G⟩,|H⟩Slaters,\displaystyle=\langle G|\rho|G\rangle,\,\,\,|\phi\rangle=\rho|G\rangle/\sqrt{\alpha}\quad|G\rangle,|H\rangle\,\,\mathrm{Slaters}, (93)
s\displaystyle s =|⟨G⁡|H⟩|,p=‖|h1⟩‖2,q=‖|h≥2⟩‖,\displaystyle=|\langle G|H\rangle|,\quad p=\||h_{1}\rangle\|^{2},\quad q=\||h_{\geq 2}\rangle\|,
w\displaystyle w =∥|ϕ≥2⟩∥,σ=ρ−|ϕ⟩⟨ϕ|,T=Trσ.\displaystyle=\||\phi_{\geq 2}\rangle\|,\,\sigma=\rho-|\phi\rangle\!\langle\phi|,\,\,\,\quad T=\Tr\sigma.

The trace of ρ\rho can be decomposed as ‖|ϕ⟩‖2+T\||\phi\rangle\|^{2}+T (note |ϕ⟩|\phi\rangle need not be unit norm), or

Tr⁡ρ=α+RG2α+w2+T=1.\Tr\rho=\alpha+\frac{R_{G}^{2}}{\alpha}+w^{2}+T=1. (94)

Since RG2/α≥0R_{G}^{2}/\alpha\geq 0 and T≥0T\geq 0, we have w2≤1−αw^{2}\leq 1-\alpha. In the regime α≥2/3\alpha\geq 2/3, we may write 1−α≤α/21-\alpha\leq\alpha/2 and hence w2≤α/2w^{2}\leq\alpha/2. Hence the bound q≤2​(1−s)q\leq\sqrt{2}(1-s) implies

w​q≤α/2⋅2​(1−s)=α​(1−s).wq\leq\sqrt{\alpha/2}\cdot\sqrt{2}(1-s)=\sqrt{\alpha}(1-s). (95)

It follows that α​s+w​q≤α\sqrt{\alpha}s+wq\leq\sqrt{\alpha} in the regime α≥2/3\alpha\geq 2/3. Now, applying Cauchy-Schwarz to each particle-hole sector (0,1,≥20,1,\geq 2) gives

|⟨H|ϕ⟩|≤α​s+RGα​p+w​q,|\langle H|\phi\rangle|\leq\sqrt{\alpha}s+\frac{R_{G}}{\sqrt{\alpha}}\sqrt{p}+wq, (96)

while σ​|G⟩=0\sigma|G\rangle=0 and ‖σ‖≤tr⁡σ\|\sigma\|\leq\operatorname{tr}\sigma give ⟨H|σ|H⟩=(⟨h1|+⟨h≥2|)​σ​(|h1⟩+|h≥2⟩)≤T⁡(p+q2)\langle H|\sigma|H\rangle=(\langle h_{1}|+\langle h_{\geq 2}|)\sigma(|h_{1}\rangle+|h_{\geq 2}\rangle)\leq T(p+q^{2}). Expanding the square, using α​s+w​q≤α\sqrt{\alpha}s+wq\leq\sqrt{\alpha} on the cross term and p≤p+q2p\leq p+q^{2}, and substituting using Eq. (94), we obtain

⟨H|ρ|H⟩\displaystyle\langle H|\rho|H\rangle (97)
≤(α​s+w​q)2+2​RG​p+RG2α​p+T⁡(p+q2)\displaystyle\leq\left(\sqrt{\alpha}s+wq\right)^{2}+2R_{G}\sqrt{p}+\frac{R_{G}^{2}}{\alpha}p+T(p+q^{2})
≤(α​s+w​q)2+(1−α−w2)​(p+q2)+2​RG​p.\displaystyle\leq\left(\sqrt{\alpha}s+wq\right)^{2}+(1-\alpha-w^{2})(p+q^{2})+2R_{G}\sqrt{p}.

We claim that the first two terms of the right-hand side satisfy

(α​s+w​q)2+(1−α−w2)​(p+q2)≤α−(3​α2−1)​(p+q2).\left(\sqrt{\alpha}s+wq\right)^{2}+(1-\alpha-w^{2})(p+q^{2})\\ \leq\alpha-\left(\frac{3\alpha}{2}-1\right)(p+q^{2}). (98)

Together with the observation that since p+q2=1−s2p+q^{2}=1-s^{2} we have p≤1−s2\sqrt{p}\leq\sqrt{1-s^{2}}, this would establish Eq. (88).

Let us now prove Eq. (98). Expanding the left-hand side and substituting s2=1−p−q2s^{2}=1-p-q^{2} reduces the above to 2​λ​s​q−λ2​p≤12​(p+q2)2\lambda sq-\lambda^{2}p\leq\frac{1}{2}(p+q^{2}), where λ≔w/α∈[0,1/2]\lambda\coloneqq w/\sqrt{\alpha}\in[0,1/\sqrt{2}]. The left-hand side is concave in λ\lambda. If its maximum over [0,1/2][0,1/\sqrt{2}] is attained at an interior stationary point, then p>0p>0 and λ=s​q/p≤1/2\lambda=sq/p\leq 1/\sqrt{2}, so the maximum value is s2​q2/p≤p/2≤12​(p+q2)s^{2}q^{2}/p\leq p/2\leq\frac{1}{2}(p+q^{2}). Otherwise, the maximum is attained at λ=1/2\lambda=1/\sqrt{2} with value 2​s​q−p/2\sqrt{2}sq-p/2. Squaring the inequality s+q/2≤1s+q/\sqrt{2}\leq 1 and substituting p=1−s2−q2p=1-s^{2}-q^{2} gives 2​s​q≤p+q2/2\sqrt{2}sq\leq p+q^{2}/2, so the value is again at most 12​(p+q2)\frac{1}{2}(p+q^{2}). This proves the inequality 2​λ​s​q−λ2​p≤12​(p+q2)2\lambda sq-\lambda^{2}p\leq\frac{1}{2}(p+q^{2}) and hence Eq. (98), which is equivalent, and establishes Eq. (88).

Moreover, if α>2/3\alpha>2/3 and RG=0R_{G}=0, then Eq. (88) gives ⟨H|ρ|H⟩<α\langle H|\rho|H\rangle<\alpha whenever |⟨G|H⟩|<1|\langle G|H\rangle|<1. This proves uniqueness of the global optimum.

Finally, setting X=1−s2X=\sqrt{1-s^{2}} and μ=3​α2−1\mu=\frac{3\alpha}{2}-1, the right-hand side of Eq. (88) is at most α+supX≥0(−μ​X2+2​RG​X)=α+RG2/μ\alpha+\sup_{X\geq 0}(-\mu X^{2}+2R_{G}X)=\alpha+R_{G}^{2}/\mu, and α≥2/3+Δ\alpha\geq 2/3+\Delta gives μ≥3​Δ/2\mu\geq 3\Delta/2, which establishes Eq. (89), concluding the proof. ∎

Since pure states are a subset of mixed states, the construction of Theorem 6 shows that the threshold 2/32/3 cannot be lowered. In conclusion, each result of the main text holds for mixed states upon replacing |⟨S|ψ⟩|2|\langle S|\psi\rangle|^{2} with ⟨S|ρ|S⟩\langle S|\rho|S\rangle wherever needed, replacing BGB_{G} with RGR_{G}, and using the classical access model in Definition 1.

Appendix C Technical lemmas

We collect various lemmas used in the proofs in this work.

Lemma 4 (Truncating from the 1-RDM).

Let ρ\rho be a density matrix in ℋn\mathcal{H}_{n} and let γ\gamma be its one-body density matrix γi​j=tr⁡(ρ​cj†​ci)\gamma_{ij}=\operatorname{tr}(\rho\,c_{j}^{\dagger}c_{i}). Let 𝒜⊆ℋ1\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{1} be a subspace with projector P𝒜P_{\mathcal{A}} and dim𝒜≥n\dim\mathcal{A}\geq n. Fix ε>0\varepsilon>0 and suppose that every orbital outside 𝒜\mathcal{A} has occupation at most ε/n\varepsilon/n,

‖(I−P𝒜)​γ​(I−P𝒜)‖≤ε/n.\|(I-P_{\mathcal{A}})\gamma(I-P_{\mathcal{A}})\|\leq\varepsilon/n. (99)

Let 𝒮𝒜\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{A}} denote the set of Slater determinants whose occupied orbitals all lie in 𝒜\mathcal{A} and define

𝖮𝖯𝖳𝒜:=max|S⟩∈𝒮𝒜⁡⟨S|ρ|S⟩.\mathsf{OPT}_{\mathcal{A}}:=\max_{|S\rangle\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{A}}}\langle S|\rho|S\rangle. (100)

Then

𝖮𝖯𝖳≤𝖮𝖯𝖳𝒜+ε.\mathsf{OPT}\leq\mathsf{OPT}_{\mathcal{A}}+\varepsilon. (101)
Proof.

Let |G⟩|G\rangle be an arbitrary nn-particle Slater determinant. Let ℒ⊆ℋ1\mathcal{L}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{1} be the occupied one-particle subspace of |G⟩|G\rangle.

After a change of basis in ℒ\mathcal{L}, we may write

|G⟩=∏α=1n(cos⁡θα​aα†+sin⁡θα​bα†)​|0⟩.|G\rangle=\prod_{\alpha=1}^{n}(\cos\theta_{\alpha}\,a_{\alpha}^{\dagger}+\sin\theta_{\alpha}\,b_{\alpha}^{\dagger})|0\rangle. (102)

where the aα†a_{\alpha}^{\dagger} and bα†b_{\alpha}^{\dagger} create orthonormal orbitals in 𝒜\mathcal{A} and 𝒜⟂\mathcal{A}^{\perp}, respectively. In words, the procedure starts with a unit vector ℓ1∈ℒ\ell_{1}\in\mathcal{L} and finds a unit vector a1∈𝒜a_{1}\in\mathcal{A} which maximizes |⟨ℓ1|a1⟩||\langle\ell_{1}|a_{1}\rangle|, calling this angle θ1\theta_{1}. One then considers the complement of ℓ1\ell_{1} in ℒ\mathcal{L} and the complement of a1a_{1} in 𝒜\mathcal{A} and repeats the procedure. The bα†b_{\alpha}^{\dagger} create orbitals corresponding to ℓα−⟨ℓα|aα⟩​aα\ell_{\alpha}-\langle\ell_{\alpha}|a_{\alpha}\rangle a_{\alpha}, if this is nonzero, and bα=0b_{\alpha}=0 otherwise.

Expanding the product in |G⟩|G\rangle produces

|G⟩=c⁡|G𝒜⟩+1−c2​|K⟩,|G\rangle=c\,|G_{\mathcal{A}}\rangle+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\,|K\rangle, (103)

where c=∏α=1ncos⁡θαc=\prod_{\alpha=1}^{n}\cos\theta_{\alpha}, |G𝒜⟩=a1†⋯an†|0⟩|G_{\mathcal{A}}\rangle=a_{1}^{\dagger}\cdots a_{n}^{\dagger}|0\rangle is the Slater determinant whose occupied orbitals lie entirely in 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and |K⟩|K\rangle is in the span of Slater determinants with at least one particle in

𝒲:=span{bα:sinθα≠0,α=1,…,n}.\mathcal{W}:=\operatorname{span}\{b_{\alpha}:\sin\theta_{\alpha}\neq 0,\alpha=1,\ldots,n\}. (104)

Let P𝒲P_{\mathcal{W}} be the one-particle projector onto 𝒲\mathcal{W}. Since 𝒲⊂𝒜⟂\mathcal{W}\subset\mathcal{A}^{\perp}, and every orbital in 𝒜⟂\mathcal{A}^{\perp} has occupation at most ε/n\varepsilon/n, we have

tr⁡(P𝒲​γ)≤dim(𝒲)​ε/n≤ε.\operatorname{tr}(P_{\mathcal{W}}\gamma)\leq\dim(\mathcal{W})\varepsilon/n\leq\varepsilon. (105)

Next, choose a basis w1,…,wrw_{1},\ldots,w_{r} of 𝒲\mathcal{W} and a basis u1,…,um−ru_{1},\ldots,u_{m-r} of 𝒲⟂\mathcal{W}^{\perp}. Let

nμ=cwμ†​cwμn_{\mu}=c_{w_{\mu}}^{\dagger}c_{w_{\mu}} (106)

be the occupation-number operator for wμw_{\mu}. Let Q^𝒲=1−∏μ=1r(1−nμ)\widehat{Q}_{\mathcal{W}}=1-\prod_{\mu=1}^{r}(1-n_{\mu}) be the many-body projector onto the subspace with at least one particle in 𝒲\mathcal{W}, and let N^𝒲=∑μ=1rnμ\widehat{N}_{\mathcal{W}}=\sum_{\mu=1}^{r}n_{\mu} be the number operator in 𝒲\mathcal{W}. In a state with N^𝒲=k\widehat{N}_{\mathcal{W}}=k, we have Q^𝒲=1\widehat{Q}_{\mathcal{W}}=1 if k≥1k\geq 1 and Q^𝒲=0\widehat{Q}_{\mathcal{W}}=0 if k=0k=0. Hence

Q^𝒲⪯N^𝒲,\widehat{Q}_{\mathcal{W}}\preceq\widehat{N}_{\mathcal{W}}, (107)

where A⪯BA\preceq B means that B−AB-A is positive semidefinite. Thus we have

tr⁡(ρ​Q^𝒲)≤tr⁡(ρ​N^𝒲)=tr⁡(P𝒲​γ).\operatorname{tr}(\rho\widehat{Q}_{\mathcal{W}})\leq\operatorname{tr}(\rho\widehat{N}_{\mathcal{W}})=\operatorname{tr}(P_{\mathcal{W}}\gamma). (108)

In the last step, we have used

∑μ=1rtr⁡(ρ​cwμ†​cwμ)=∑μ=1r∑i​j(wμ)i∗​(wμ)j​tr⁡(ρ​cj†​ci).\sum_{\mu=1}^{r}\operatorname{tr}(\rho c_{w_{\mu}}^{\dagger}c_{w_{\mu}})=\sum_{\mu=1}^{r}\sum_{ij}(w_{\mu})_{i}^{*}(w_{\mu})_{j}\operatorname{tr}(\rho c_{j}^{\dagger}c_{i}). (109)

Thus

tr⁡(ρ​Q^𝒲)≤ε,\operatorname{tr}(\rho\widehat{Q}_{\mathcal{W}})\leq\varepsilon, (110)

i.e. the overlap of ρ\rho with the subspace with at least one particle in 𝒲\mathcal{W} is upper bounded by ε\varepsilon. Since |K⟩|K\rangle is supported entirely on this subspace (Q𝒲​|K⟩=|K⟩Q_{\mathcal{W}}|K\rangle=|K\rangle) we have

⟨K|ρ|K⟩=⟨K|Q𝒲​ρ​Q𝒲|K⟩≤tr⁡(ρ​Q𝒲)≤ε.\langle K|\rho|K\rangle=\langle K|Q_{\mathcal{W}}\rho Q_{\mathcal{W}}|K\rangle\leq\operatorname{tr}(\rho Q_{\mathcal{W}})\leq\varepsilon. (111)

Next, we expand

⟨G|ρ|G⟩\displaystyle\langle G|\rho|G\rangle =c2​⟨G𝒜|ρ|G𝒜⟩+(1−c2)​⟨K|ρ|K⟩\displaystyle=c^{2}\langle G_{\mathcal{A}}|\rho|G_{\mathcal{A}}\rangle+(1-c^{2})\langle K|\rho|K\rangle
+2​c​1−c2​Re⁡⟨G𝒜|ρ|K⟩.\displaystyle\quad+2c\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\,\operatorname{Re}\langle G_{\mathcal{A}}|\rho|K\rangle. (112)

Since ρ⪰0\rho\succeq 0 defines a Hermitian form, Cauchy–Schwarz gives

|⟨G𝒜|ρ|K⟩|≤⟨G𝒜|ρ|G𝒜⟩​⟨K|ρ|K⟩|\langle G_{\mathcal{A}}|\rho|K\rangle|\leq\sqrt{\langle G_{\mathcal{A}}|\rho|G_{\mathcal{A}}\rangle\langle K|\rho|K\rangle} (113)

and hence

⟨G|ρ|G⟩≤(c​⟨G𝒜|ρ|G𝒜⟩+1−c2​⟨K|ρ|K⟩)2.\langle G|\rho|G\rangle\leq\left(c\sqrt{\langle G_{\mathcal{A}}|\rho|G_{\mathcal{A}}\rangle}+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\sqrt{\langle K|\rho|K\rangle}\right)^{2}. (114)

Next, we use ⟨G𝒜|ρ|G𝒜⟩≤𝖮𝖯𝖳𝒜\langle G_{\mathcal{A}}|\rho|G_{\mathcal{A}}\rangle\leq\mathsf{OPT}_{\mathcal{A}} and Eq. (111) to write

⟨G|ρ|G⟩≤(c​𝖮𝖯𝖳𝒜+1−c2​ε)2.\langle G|\rho|G\rangle\leq\left(c\sqrt{\mathsf{OPT}_{\mathcal{A}}}+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\sqrt{\varepsilon}\right)^{2}. (115)

Next, applying Cauchy-Schwarz to the real vectors (c,1−c2)(c,\sqrt{1-c^{2}}) and (𝖮𝖯𝖳𝒜,ε)(\sqrt{\mathsf{OPT}_{\mathcal{A}}},\sqrt{\varepsilon}) gives us

⟨G|ρ|G⟩\displaystyle\langle G|\rho|G\rangle ≤𝖮𝖯𝖳𝒜+ε.\displaystyle\leq\mathsf{OPT}_{\mathcal{A}}+\varepsilon. (116)

Since |G⟩|G\rangle was an arbitrary Slater,

𝖮𝖯𝖳≤𝖮𝖯𝖳𝒜+ε.\mathsf{OPT}\leq\mathsf{OPT}_{\mathcal{A}}+\varepsilon. (117)

∎

The estimator for the 1-RDM γ\gamma may be noisy. The next lemma shows that the active-space truncation of Lemma 4 is robust to noise. The key idea is that only the subspace 𝒜\mathcal{A}, not a particular choice of basis of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, needs to be moderately robust to noise in order for the truncation of the 1-RDM to be useful.

Lemma 5 (Truncating from a noisy 1-RDM).

In the setting of Lemma 4, let γ^\hat{\gamma} be a Hermitian matrix estimating the 1-RDM γ\gamma with error ‖γ^−γ‖≤η\|\hat{\gamma}-\gamma\|\leq\eta. Fix a threshold τ^>η\hat{\tau}>\eta and let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be the span of the eigenvectors ψ^a\hat{\psi}^{a} of γ^\hat{\gamma} whose eigenvalues exceed τ^\hat{\tau}, i.e. 𝒜=span⁡{ψ^a∣ν^a>τ^}\mathcal{A}=\operatorname{span}\{\hat{\psi}^{a}\mid\hat{\nu}_{a}>\hat{\tau}\}. Let P𝒜P_{\mathcal{A}} be a projector onto 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Then 𝒜\mathcal{A} satisfies the hypothesis of Lemma 4 with

‖(I−P𝒜)​γ​(I−P𝒜)‖≤τ^+η\|(I-P_{\mathcal{A}})\gamma(I-P_{\mathcal{A}})\|\leq\hat{\tau}+\eta (118)

and dim𝒜≤nτ^−η\dim\mathcal{A}\leq\frac{n}{\hat{\tau}-\eta}. In particular, taking η=ε/4​n\eta=\varepsilon/4n and τ^=3​ε/4​n\hat{\tau}=3\varepsilon/4n gives ‖(I−P𝒜)​γ​(I−P𝒜)‖≤ε/n\|(I-P_{\mathcal{A}})\gamma(I-P_{\mathcal{A}})\|\leq\varepsilon/n and dim𝒜≤2​n2/ε\dim\mathcal{A}\leq 2n^{2}/\varepsilon, so that 𝖮𝖯𝖳≤𝖮𝖯𝖳𝒜+ε\mathsf{OPT}\leq\mathsf{OPT}_{\mathcal{A}}+\varepsilon with dim𝒜=O⁡(n2/ε)\dim\mathcal{A}=O(n^{2}/\varepsilon).

Furthermore, an estimator γ^\hat{\gamma} satisfying ‖γ^−γ‖≤η\|\hat{\gamma}-\gamma\|\leq\eta with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta can be obtained from

nfcs=O⁡(m2​log⁡(m/δ)η2)n_{\mathrm{fcs}}=O\left(\frac{m^{2}\log(m/\delta)}{\eta^{2}}\right) (119)

quantum copies of ρ\rho via fermionic classical shadows [76].

Proof.

Let vv be a unit vector outside 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Then vv lies in the span of the eigenvectors of γ^\hat{\gamma} with eigenvalue at most τ^\hat{\tau}, so ⟨v|γ^|v⟩≤τ^\langle v|\hat{\gamma}|v\rangle\leq\hat{\tau}. Hence

⟨v|γ|v⟩=⟨v|γ^​|v⟩−⟨v|​(γ^−γ)|v⟩≤τ^+η.\langle v|\gamma|v\rangle=\langle v|\hat{\gamma}|v\rangle-\langle v|(\hat{\gamma}-\gamma)|v\rangle\leq\hat{\tau}+\eta. (120)

Since γ⪰0\gamma\succeq 0, the operator norm of (I−P𝒜)​γ​(I−P𝒜)(I-P_{\mathcal{A}})\gamma(I-P_{\mathcal{A}}) is the maximum of ⟨v|γ|v⟩\langle v|\gamma|v\rangle over unit vectors vv outside 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and so ‖(I−P𝒜)​γ​(I−P𝒜)‖≤τ^+η\|(I-P_{\mathcal{A}})\gamma(I-P_{\mathcal{A}})\|\leq\hat{\tau}+\eta.

Next we bound the dimension of 𝒜\mathcal{A}. The sorted eigenvalues of γ^\hat{\gamma} and γ\gamma satisfy ν^a≤νa+η\hat{\nu}_{a}\leq\nu_{a}+\eta, so every ν^a>τ^\hat{\nu}_{a}>\hat{\tau} has νa>τ^−η\nu_{a}>\hat{\tau}-\eta. The number of such orbitals is at most tr⁡γ/(τ^−η)=n/(τ^−η)\operatorname{tr}\gamma/(\hat{\tau}-\eta)=n/(\hat{\tau}-\eta), since γ⪰0\gamma\succeq 0 and tr⁡γ=n\operatorname{tr}\gamma=n. Hence dim𝒜≤n/(τ^−η)\dim\mathcal{A}\leq n/(\hat{\tau}-\eta). Both bounds hold for the stated η\eta and τ^\hat{\tau}, and 𝖮𝖯𝖳≤𝖮𝖯𝖳𝒜+ε\mathsf{OPT}\leq\mathsf{OPT}_{\mathcal{A}}+\varepsilon then follows from Lemma 4.

We next justify Eq. (119). The fermionic classical shadow formalism provides single-shot estimators γ^(s)\hat{\gamma}^{(s)} which are Hermitian m×mm\times m matrices satisfying 𝔼⁡[γ^(s)]=γ\mathbb{E}[\hat{\gamma}^{(s)}]=\gamma. We consider averaging NN of them to obtain an estimator γ^≔1N​∑s=1Nγ^(s)\hat{\gamma}\coloneqq\frac{1}{N}\sum_{s=1}^{N}\hat{\gamma}^{(s)}. By Ref. [76] (in particular Eq. (13) and ensuing discussion), we have the “shadow norm”

‖γ^(s)‖≤1/λm,1≡(2​m2)(m1)=2​m−1.\|\hat{\gamma}^{(s)}\|\leq 1/\lambda_{m,1}\equiv\frac{\binom{2m}{2}}{\binom{m}{1}}=2m-1. (121)

We next apply a matrix concentration inequality [61, 62]. Defining centered snapshots Xs≔γ^(s)−γX_{s}\coloneqq\hat{\gamma}^{(s)}-\gamma, which satisfy 𝔼⁡[Xs]=0\mathbb{E}[X_{s}]=0, ‖Xs‖≤2​m\|X_{s}\|\leq 2m, and ‖𝔼⁡[Xs2]‖≤𝔼​‖Xs‖2≤(2​m)2\|\mathbb{E}[X_{s}^{2}]\|\leq\mathbb{E}\|X_{s}\|^{2}\leq(2m)^{2}. Then the matrix Bernstein inequality yields

Pr[∥γ^−γ∥≥η]≤2mexp(−c​N​η2m2)\mathrm{Pr}\left[\|\hat{\gamma}-\gamma\|\geq\eta\right]\leq 2m\exp\left(-\frac{cN\eta^{2}}{m^{2}}\right) (122)

for a universal O⁡(1)O(1) constant c>0c>0. In words, the probability that ‖γ^−γ‖≥η\|\hat{\gamma}-\gamma\|\geq\eta decays exponentially with N​η2/m2N\eta^{2}/m^{2}. Hence ‖γ^−γ‖≤η\|\hat{\gamma}-\gamma\|\leq\eta holds with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta as long as N=O⁡(m2​log⁡(m/δ)/η2)N=O(m^{2}\log(m/\delta)/\eta^{2}), as was to be shown. ∎

The following lemma is a useful technical result on the closest Slater to a superposition of two Slaters.

Lemma 6 (Superpositions of Slaters).

Let |E⟩|E\rangle and |F⟩|F\rangle be nn-particle Slater determinants whose occupied one-particle subspaces ℰ,ℱ⊆ℋ1\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{1} are orthogonal. Assume n≥2n\geq 2. Then for every nn-particle Slater determinant |G⟩|G\rangle, we have

|⟨E|G⟩|+|⟨F|G⟩|≤1.|\langle E|G\rangle|+|\langle F|G\rangle|\leq 1. (123)

Moreover, consider a superposition of the form

|ψ⟩=|E⟩+α​|F⟩1+|α|2|\psi\rangle=\frac{|E\rangle+\alpha|F\rangle}{\sqrt{1+|\alpha|^{2}}} (124)

for |α|>1|\alpha|>1. The unique Slater determinant with maximal fidelity with |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle is |F⟩|F\rangle (up to phase), with fidelity |α|2/(1+|α|2)|\alpha|^{2}/(1+|\alpha|^{2}).

Proof.

Choose orthonormal bases e1,…,ene_{1},\ldots,e_{n} of ℰ\mathcal{E} and f1,…,fnf_{1},\ldots,f_{n} of ℱ\mathcal{F}, so that

|E⟩=ce1†⋯cen†|0⟩,|F⟩=cf1†⋯cfn†|0⟩.|E\rangle=c_{e_{1}}^{\dagger}\cdots c_{e_{n}}^{\dagger}|0\rangle,\qquad|F\rangle=c_{f_{1}}^{\dagger}\cdots c_{f_{n}}^{\dagger}|0\rangle. (125)

Let |G⟩|G\rangle be an arbitrary Slater and choose an orthonormal basis g1,…,gng_{1},\ldots,g_{n} such that |G⟩=cg1†⋯cgn†|0⟩|G\rangle=c_{g_{1}}^{\dagger}\cdots c_{g_{n}}^{\dagger}|0\rangle. Define the overlap matrices Mμ​α(E|G)=⟨eμ|gα⟩M^{(E|G)}_{\mu\alpha}=\langle e_{\mu}|g_{\alpha}\rangle, Mμ​α(F|G)=⟨fμ|gα⟩M^{(F|G)}_{\mu\alpha}=\langle f_{\mu}|g_{\alpha}\rangle, so

⟨E|G⟩=detM(E|G),⟨F|G⟩=detM(F|G).\langle E|G\rangle=\det M^{(E|G)},\quad\langle F|G\rangle=\det M^{(F|G)}. (126)

Since ℰ⟂ℱ\mathcal{E}\perp\mathcal{F}, each unit vector gαg_{\alpha} satisfies

∑μ=1n(|⟨eμ|gα⟩|2+|⟨fμ|gα⟩|2)≤1.\sum_{\mu=1}^{n}\left(|\langle e_{\mu}|g_{\alpha}\rangle|^{2}+|\langle f_{\mu}|g_{\alpha}\rangle|^{2}\right)\leq 1. (127)

Summing over α\alpha gives

∑μ,α=1n(|Mμ​α(E|G)|2+|Mμ​α(F|G)|2)≤n.\sum_{\mu,\alpha=1}^{n}\left(|M^{(E|G)}_{\mu\alpha}|^{2}+|M^{(F|G)}_{\mu\alpha}|^{2}\right)\leq n. (128)

We define the average weights

uE=1n​∑μ,α|Mμ​α(E|G)|2,uF=1n​∑μ,α|Mμ​α(F|G)|2.u_{E}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{\mu,\alpha}|M_{\mu\alpha}^{(E|G)}|^{2},\quad u_{F}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{\mu,\alpha}|M_{\mu\alpha}^{(F|G)}|^{2}. (129)

which satisfy uE+uF≤1u_{E}+u_{F}\leq 1 and uE,uF≥0u_{E},u_{F}\geq 0. Next, we define singular values {sαA}α=1n\{s_{\alpha}^{A}\}_{\alpha=1}^{n} for M(A|G)M^{(A|G)} for A=E,FA=E,F, such that

|detM(A|G)|=∏α=1n|sαA|.|\det M^{(A|G)}|=\prod_{\alpha=1}^{n}|s_{\alpha}^{A}|. (130)

In terms of these singular values, we have

uA=1n​∑α=1n|sαA|2.u_{A}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{n}|s_{\alpha}^{A}|^{2}. (131)

Next, we apply the AM–GM inequality to the set of numbers {|sαA|2}\{|s_{\alpha}^{A}|^{2}\}, yielding

(∏α=1n|sαA|2)1/n≤1n​∑α=1n|sαA|2=uA.\left(\prod_{\alpha=1}^{n}|s_{\alpha}^{A}|^{2}\right)^{1/n}\leq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{n}|s_{\alpha}^{A}|^{2}=u_{A}. (132)

Raising both sides to the power of n/2n/2 yields |detM(A|G)|≤uAn/2|\det M^{(A|G)}|\leq u_{A}^{n/2}. Hence |⟨A|G⟩|≤uAn/2≤uA|\langle A|G\rangle|\leq u_{A}^{n/2}\leq u_{A} for A=E,FA=E,F, where in the last step we have used that n≥2n\geq 2 and 0≤uA≤10\leq u_{A}\leq 1. Finally, we conclude that

|⟨E|G⟩|+|⟨F|G⟩|≤uE+uF≤1,|\langle E|G\rangle|+|\langle F|G\rangle|\leq u_{E}+u_{F}\leq 1, (133)

as was to be shown. This bounds the overlap of an arbitrary Slater |G⟩|G\rangle with an orthogonal pair of Slaters |E⟩|E\rangle and |F⟩|F\rangle.

Next, we consider the state |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle defined in Eq. (124). Let |G⟩|G\rangle again be an arbitrary Slater and write xE=|⟨E|G⟩|x_{E}=|\langle E|G\rangle| and xF=|⟨F|G⟩|x_{F}=|\langle F|G\rangle|. Without loss of generality, we assume α>0\alpha>0, so that

|⟨G|ψ⟩|≤xE+α​xF1+α2.|\langle G|\psi\rangle|\leq\frac{x_{E}+\alpha x_{F}}{\sqrt{1+\alpha^{2}}}. (134)

Because α>1\alpha>1 by assumption, the numerator is maximized over the domain {xE,xF≥0:xE+xF≤1}\{x_{E},x_{F}\geq 0:\ x_{E}+x_{F}\leq 1\} at precisely (xE,xF)=(0,1)(x_{E},x_{F})=(0,1), yielding

|⟨G|ψ⟩|≤α1+α2.|\langle G|\psi\rangle|\leq\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{1+\alpha^{2}}}. (135)

This bound is attained when xF=|⟨F|G⟩|=1x_{F}=|\langle F|G\rangle|=1, which means |G⟩=|F⟩|G\rangle=|F\rangle as nn-particle Slater determinants, up to an overall phase. Thus |F⟩|F\rangle is the unique closest Slater, up to phase. ∎

The following Lemma identifies single particle-hole excitations as the tangent directions of the manifold of Slater determinants, following Refs. [60, 56]. The stationarity condition for the fidelity mirrors the classic Brillouin condition for the stationarity of the variational Hartree-Fock energy [12], and hence we refer to the following as the Brillouin condition for fidelity.

Lemma 7 (Brillouin condition for fidelity).

Let

|G⟩=cg1†⋯cgn†|0⟩|G\rangle=c_{g_{1}}^{\dagger}\cdots c_{g_{n}}^{\dagger}|0\rangle (136)

be a Slater determinant with occupied orbitals g1,…,gng_{1},\ldots,g_{n} and unoccupied orbitals {fa}\{f_{a}\} with corresponding creation operators cfa†c_{f_{a}}^{\dagger}, for a=1,…,m−na=1,\ldots,m-n. Let

|Ga​α⟩=cfa†​cgα​|G⟩|G_{a\alpha}\rangle=c_{f_{a}}^{\dagger}c_{g_{\alpha}}|G\rangle (137)

denote the single particle-hole excitations on top of |G⟩|G\rangle. For a normalized nn-fermion state |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle, define

F⁡(G)=|⟨G|ψ⟩|2,BG2=∑a,α|⟨Ga​α|ψ⟩|2≥0.\mathrm{F}(G)=|\langle G|\psi\rangle|^{2},\qquad B_{G}^{2}=\sum_{a,\alpha}|\langle G_{a\alpha}|\psi\rangle|^{2}\geq 0. (138)

Then the first variation of F\mathrm{F} at |G⟩|G\rangle vanishes if and only if

⟨G|ψ⟩​⟨Ga​α|ψ⟩=0\langle G|\psi\rangle\,\langle G_{a\alpha}|\psi\rangle=0 (139)

for all a,αa,\alpha. In particular, if F⁡(G)>0\mathrm{F}(G)>0, then GG is a stationary point if and only if

BG=0.B_{G}=0. (140)
Proof.

We first establish some basic facts about the tangent space of the manifold of Slater determinants near |G⟩|G\rangle (referring to e.g. Ref. [23] for further details). The tangent space is the space of derivatives, at |G⟩|G\rangle, of smooth paths in the manifold that pass through |G⟩|G\rangle. Thus we consider a path

|G(τ)⟩=cg1†(τ)⋯cgn†(τ)|0⟩,|G(\tau)\rangle=c_{g_{1}}^{\dagger}(\tau)\cdots c_{g_{n}}^{\dagger}(\tau)|0\rangle, (141)

where cgα†​(0)=cgα†c_{g_{\alpha}}^{\dagger}(0)=c_{g_{\alpha}}^{\dagger}, and where the orbitals g1​(τ),…,gn​(τ)g_{1}(\tau),\ldots,g_{n}(\tau) remain orthonormal for all τ\tau. In a fixed one-particle basis, each creation operator has the form

cgα†​(τ)=∑i𝒢α​i​(τ)​ci†.c_{g_{\alpha}}^{\dagger}(\tau)=\sum_{i}\mathcal{G}_{\alpha i}(\tau)c_{i}^{\dagger}. (142)

The derivative of cgα†​(τ)c_{g_{\alpha}}^{\dagger}(\tau) is therefore:

c˙gα†:=dd​τ​cgα†​(τ)|τ=0=∑i𝒢α​i′​(0)​ci†.\dot{c}_{g_{\alpha}}^{\dagger}:=\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\tau}c_{g_{\alpha}}^{\dagger}(\tau)\right|_{\tau=0}=\sum_{i}\mathcal{G}^{\prime}_{\alpha i}(0)c_{i}^{\dagger}. (143)

Since the occupied orbitals gαg_{\alpha} together with the unoccupied orbitals faf_{a} form an orthonormal basis of the one-particle Hilbert space, we may write

c˙gα†=∑β=1nAβ​α​cgβ†+∑aTa​α​cfa†.\dot{c}_{g_{\alpha}}^{\dagger}=\sum_{\beta=1}^{n}A_{\beta\alpha}c_{g_{\beta}}^{\dagger}+\sum_{a}T_{a\alpha}c_{f_{a}}^{\dagger}. (144)

Orthonormality for all τ\tau imposes the following constraint. Since ⟨gβ​(τ)|gα​(τ)⟩=δβ​α\langle g_{\beta}(\tau)|g_{\alpha}(\tau)\rangle=\delta_{\beta\alpha}, we have ⟨g˙β|gα⟩+⟨gβ|g˙α⟩=0\langle\dot{g}_{\beta}|g_{\alpha}\rangle+\langle g_{\beta}|\dot{g}_{\alpha}\rangle=0, and hence taking Aβ​α=⟨gβ|g˙α⟩A_{\beta\alpha}=\langle g_{\beta}|\dot{g}_{\alpha}\rangle, this becomes

A†=−A,A^{\dagger}=-A, (145)

i.e. AA is anti-Hermitian. Next, differentiating the many-body Slater determinant gives us

dd​τ|G(τ)⟩|τ=0=∑α=1ncg1†⋯c˙gα†⋯cgn†|0⟩.\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\tau}|G(\tau)\rangle\right|_{\tau=0}=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{n}c_{g_{1}}^{\dagger}\cdots\dot{c}_{g_{\alpha}}^{\dagger}\cdots c_{g_{n}}^{\dagger}|0\rangle. (146)

Substituting c˙gα†\dot{c}_{g_{\alpha}}^{\dagger} gives one term involving AA and one term involving TT. The term involving AA has the form

∑α,βAβ​αcg1†⋯cgβ†⋯cgn†|0⟩,\sum_{\alpha,\beta}A_{\beta\alpha}c_{g_{1}}^{\dagger}\cdots c_{g_{\beta}}^{\dagger}\cdots c_{g_{n}}^{\dagger}|0\rangle, (147)

where cgβ†c_{g_{\beta}}^{\dagger} replaces cgα†c_{g_{\alpha}}^{\dagger}. If β≠α\beta\neq\alpha, this contains two identical creation operators and hence vanishes by fermionic antisymmetry. Thus only the terms with β=α\beta=\alpha survive, giving

∑α=1nAα​α​|G⟩=tr⁡(A)​|G⟩.\sum_{\alpha=1}^{n}A_{\alpha\alpha}|G\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(A)|G\rangle. (148)

Since AA is anti-Hermitian, tr⁡(A)\operatorname{tr}(A) is purely imaginary. This term corresponds to infinitesimal phase rotation of |G⟩|G\rangle. The term involving TT gives

∑a,αTa​αcg1†⋯cfa†⋯cgn†|0⟩\sum_{a,\alpha}T_{a\alpha}\,c_{g_{1}}^{\dagger}\cdots c_{f_{a}}^{\dagger}\cdots c_{g_{n}}^{\dagger}|0\rangle (149)

where cfa†c_{f_{a}}^{\dagger} replaces cgα†c_{g_{\alpha}}^{\dagger}. This is a single particle-hole excitation

cg1†⋯cfa†⋯cgn†|0⟩=cfa†cgα|G⟩=|Ga​α⟩,c_{g_{1}}^{\dagger}\cdots c_{f_{a}}^{\dagger}\cdots c_{g_{n}}^{\dagger}|0\rangle=c_{f_{a}}^{\dagger}c_{g_{\alpha}}|G\rangle=|G_{a\alpha}\rangle, (150)

up to the sign convention fixed by the ordering of the creation operators. Therefore every tangent vector has the form

dd​τ​|G⁡(τ)⟩|τ=0=i​θ​|G⟩+∑a,αTa​α​|Ga​α⟩,\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\tau}|G(\tau)\rangle\right|_{\tau=0}=i\theta|G\rangle+\sum_{a,\alpha}T_{a\alpha}|G_{a\alpha}\rangle, (151)

and the |Ga​α⟩|G_{a\alpha}\rangle furnish a basis for the tangent space.

As a consistency check, we may compare the dimension of the tangent space to the dimension of the manifold of Slater determinants. A Slater determinant is specified by an nn-dimensional subspace inside the mm-dimensional single-particle Hilbert space. The former can be specified by (the first nn columns of) a U⁡(m)U(m) unitary, but rotations within the subspace or its complement do not change the state, and hence we must mod out by U⁡(n)U(n) and U⁡(m−n)U(m-n) rotations. Since the real dimension of U⁡(d)U(d) is d2d^{2}, the real dimension of the Slater manifold (i.e. Grassmannian) is m2−n2−(m−n)2=2​n​(m−n)m^{2}-n^{2}-(m-n)^{2}=2n(m-n) and the complex dimension is n⁡(m−n)n(m-n). Likewise, Ta​αT_{a\alpha} is an n×(m−n)n\times(m-n) complex matrix, and hence the dimensions match.

Now that we have identified the tangent directions at |G⟩|G\rangle, we may derive the first variation of F⁡(G)\mathrm{F}(G) by considering a path of the form

|G⁡(τ)⟩=|G⟩+τ​∑a,αTa​α​|Ga​α⟩+O⁡(τ2).|G(\tau)\rangle=|G\rangle+\tau\sum_{a,\alpha}T_{a\alpha}|G_{a\alpha}\rangle+O(\tau^{2}). (152)

Defining Ba​α=⟨Ga​α|ψ⟩,B_{a\alpha}=\langle G_{a\alpha}|\psi\rangle, we have

⟨G⁡(τ)|ψ⟩=⟨G|ψ⟩+τ​∑a,αTa​α¯​Ba​α+O⁡(τ2),\langle G(\tau)|\psi\rangle=\langle G|\psi\rangle+\tau\sum_{a,\alpha}\overline{T_{a\alpha}}\,B_{a\alpha}+O(\tau^{2}), (153)

and therefore

F⁡(G⁡(τ))\displaystyle\mathrm{F}(G(\tau)) =|⟨G⁡(τ)|ψ⟩|2\displaystyle=|\langle G(\tau)|\psi\rangle|^{2}
=|⟨G|ψ⟩|2+2​τ​Re⁡[⟨ψ|G⟩​∑a,αTa​α¯​Ba​α]+O⁡(τ2).\displaystyle=|\langle G|\psi\rangle|^{2}+2\tau\operatorname{Re}\left[\langle\psi|G\rangle\sum_{a,\alpha}\overline{T_{a\alpha}}\,B_{a\alpha}\right]+O(\tau^{2}). (154)

Since each Ta​αT_{a\alpha} is arbitrary, the first variation vanishes if and only if

⟨ψ|G⟩​Ba​α=0\langle\psi|G\rangle B_{a\alpha}=0 (155)

for every a,αa,\alpha. Hence, if F⁡(G)>0\mathrm{F}(G)>0, then ⟨G|ψ⟩≠0\langle G|\psi\rangle\neq 0, and this reduces to

⟨Ga​α|ψ⟩=0∀a,α\langle G_{a\alpha}|\psi\rangle=0\qquad\forall a,\alpha (156)

which is equivalent to BG2=∑a,α|⟨Ga​α|ψ⟩|2=0B_{G}^{2}=\sum_{a,\alpha}|\langle G_{a\alpha}|\psi\rangle|^{2}=0, as was to be shown. ∎

Lemma 8 (Bounding higher particle-hole excitations).

Let |G⟩|G\rangle and |H⟩|H\rangle be normalized nn-particle Slater determinants. Let

|G⟩=cg1†⋯cgn†|0⟩|G\rangle=c_{g_{1}}^{\dagger}\cdots c_{g_{n}}^{\dagger}|0\rangle (157)

have occupied orbitals g1,…,gng_{1},\ldots,g_{n} and unoccupied orbitals {fa}\{f_{a}\} with corresponding creation operators cfa†c_{f_{a}}^{\dagger}, for a=1,…,m−na=1,\ldots,m-n. Decompose |H⟩|H\rangle into particle-hole sectors relative to |G⟩|G\rangle:

|H⟩=|h0⟩+|h1⟩+|h≥2⟩,|H\rangle=|h_{0}\rangle+|h_{1}\rangle+|h_{\geq 2}\rangle, (158)

where |h0⟩|h_{0}\rangle is proportional to |G⟩|G\rangle, |h1⟩|h_{1}\rangle lies in the span of the single particle-hole excitations cfa†​cgα​|G⟩c_{f_{a}}^{\dagger}c_{g_{\alpha}}|G\rangle and |h≥2⟩|h_{\geq 2}\rangle contains all two-and-higher particle-hole sectors. Write

s=‖|h0⟩‖=|⟨G|H⟩|,q=‖|h≥2⟩‖.s=\left\||h_{0}\rangle\right\|=|\langle G|H\rangle|,\qquad q=\left\||h_{\geq 2}\rangle\right\|. (159)

Then

q≤2​(1−s).q\leq\sqrt{2}(1-s). (160)
Proof.

This proof borrows some mathematical steps from Ref. [8], though we present it in a self-contained manner. If s=0s=0, then q≤1≤2q\leq 1\leq\sqrt{2}, and the result is immediate, so we assume s>0s>0 in the following. We write

|G⟩=cg1†⋯cgn†|0⟩,|H⟩=ch1†⋯chn†|0⟩,|G\rangle=c_{g_{1}}^{\dagger}\cdots c_{g_{n}}^{\dagger}|0\rangle,\qquad|H\rangle=c_{h_{1}}^{\dagger}\cdots c_{h_{n}}^{\dagger}|0\rangle, (161)

where g1,…,gng_{1},\ldots,g_{n} and h1,…,hnh_{1},\ldots,h_{n} are orthonormal occupied orbitals for |G⟩|G\rangle and |H⟩|H\rangle, respectively, and define the overlap matrix

Mα​β(G|H)=⟨gα|hβ⟩.M^{(G|H)}_{\alpha\beta}=\langle g_{\alpha}|h_{\beta}\rangle. (162)

Taking a singular value decomposition of M(G|H)M^{(G|H)} and rotating the occupied bases of |G⟩|G\rangle and |H⟩|H\rangle accordingly, we may assume that

Mα​β(G|H)=σα​δα​βM^{(G|H)}_{\alpha\beta}=\sigma_{\alpha}\delta_{\alpha\beta} (163)

with singular values 0≤σα≤10\leq\sigma_{\alpha}\leq 1. Since

s=|⟨G|H⟩|=|detM(G|H)|=∏α=1nσαs=|\langle G|H\rangle|=|\det M^{(G|H)}|=\prod_{\alpha=1}^{n}\sigma_{\alpha} (164)

and s>0s>0, all σα\sigma_{\alpha} are nonzero. We write

σα=cos⁡θα,0≤θα<π2.\sigma_{\alpha}=\cos\theta_{\alpha},\qquad 0\leq\theta_{\alpha}<\frac{\pi}{2}. (165)

For each α\alpha with θα>0\theta_{\alpha}>0, we may define an unoccupied orbital of |G⟩|G\rangle by

fα=hα−cos⁡θα​gαsin⁡θα.f_{\alpha}=\frac{h_{\alpha}-\cos\theta_{\alpha}\,g_{\alpha}}{\sin\theta_{\alpha}}. (166)

If sin⁡θα=0\sin\theta_{\alpha}=0, the choice of fαf_{\alpha} will be irrelevant. The orbitals fαf_{\alpha} are orthonormal and orthogonal to the occupied orbitals of |G⟩|G\rangle. Thus the occupied orbitals of |H⟩|H\rangle can be written as hα=cos⁡θα​gα+sin⁡θα​fα.h_{\alpha}=\cos\theta_{\alpha}\,g_{\alpha}+\sin\theta_{\alpha}\,f_{\alpha}. Equivalently,

|H⟩=∏α=1n(cos⁡θα​cgα†+sin⁡θα​cfα†)​|0⟩.|H\rangle=\prod_{\alpha=1}^{n}\left(\cos\theta_{\alpha}\,c_{g_{\alpha}}^{\dagger}+\sin\theta_{\alpha}\,c_{f_{\alpha}}^{\dagger}\right)|0\rangle. (167)

We now expand this product to obtain a particle-hole decomposition of |H⟩|H\rangle relative to |G⟩|G\rangle (as in Fig. 8). First, the term with no ff orbitals is precisely |h0⟩|h_{0}\rangle and satisfies

‖|h0⟩‖2=s2=∏α=1ncos2⁡θα.\left\||h_{0}\rangle\right\|^{2}=s^{2}=\prod_{\alpha=1}^{n}\cos^{2}\theta_{\alpha}. (168)

Next, the terms with exactly one ff orbital add up to give |h1⟩|h_{1}\rangle, and hence we have

‖|h1⟩‖2=∑α=1nsin2⁡θα​∏β≠αcos2⁡θβ.\left\||h_{1}\rangle\right\|^{2}=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{n}\sin^{2}\theta_{\alpha}\prod_{\beta\neq\alpha}\cos^{2}\theta_{\beta}. (169)

It is useful to set rα=tan2⁡θα.r_{\alpha}=\tan^{2}\theta_{\alpha}. Then

‖|h1⟩‖2=s2​∑α=1nrα.\left\||h_{1}\rangle\right\|^{2}=s^{2}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{n}r_{\alpha}. (170)

Finally, all remaining terms add up to give |h≥2⟩|h_{\geq 2}\rangle. Since |H⟩|H\rangle is normalized, we have

q2\displaystyle q^{2} =‖|h≥2⟩‖2=1−‖|h0⟩‖2−‖|h1⟩‖2\displaystyle=\left\||h_{\geq 2}\rangle\right\|^{2}=1-\left\||h_{0}\rangle\right\|^{2}-\left\||h_{1}\rangle\right\|^{2}
=1−s2​(1+∑α=1nrα).\displaystyle=1-s^{2}\left(1+\sum_{\alpha=1}^{n}r_{\alpha}\right). (171)

Next, we lower bound ∑αrα\sum_{\alpha}r_{\alpha} in terms of ss. For r≥0r\geq 0, we have r≥log⁡(1+r)r\geq\log(1+r). Hence

∑α=1nrα≥∑α=1nlog⁡(1+rα).\sum_{\alpha=1}^{n}r_{\alpha}\geq\sum_{\alpha=1}^{n}\log(1+r_{\alpha}). (172)

Using s2=∏α=1ncos2⁡θα=∏α=1n(1+rα)−1,s^{2}=\prod_{\alpha=1}^{n}\cos^{2}\theta_{\alpha}=\prod_{\alpha=1}^{n}(1+r_{\alpha})^{-1}, we get

∑α=1nlog⁡(1+rα)=−log⁡s2=−2​log⁡s\sum_{\alpha=1}^{n}\log(1+r_{\alpha})=-\log s^{2}=-2\log s (173)

and therefore q2≤1−s2​(1−2​log⁡s).q^{2}\leq 1-s^{2}(1-2\log s). It remains to show that the right-hand side is bounded by 2​(1−s)22(1-s)^{2}. Define

g⁡(s)=2​(1−s)2−(1−s2​(1−2​log⁡s)).g(s)=2(1-s)^{2}-(1-s^{2}(1-2\log s)). (174)

We claim g⁡(s)≥0g(s)\geq 0 on the interval 0<s≤10<s\leq 1. For an elementary proof, note that g⁡(1)=0g(1)=0 and g′​(s)=4​(s−1−s​log⁡s)≤0g^{\prime}(s)=4(s-1-s\log s)\leq 0 on this interval. Since gg decreases as ss increases to 11 and g⁡(1)=0g(1)=0, we have g⁡(s)≥0g(s)\geq 0. Hence 1−s2​(1−2​log⁡s)≤2​(1−s)2,1-s^{2}(1-2\log s)\leq 2(1-s)^{2}, which combines with the previous bound to give us

q2≤2​(1−s)2.q^{2}\leq 2(1-s)^{2}. (175)

Taking square roots proves the claim. ∎

Lemma 9 (Agnostic quantum threshold search).

Let A1,…,AMA_{1},\ldots,A_{M} be known observables with 0⪯Ai⪯10\preceq A_{i}\preceq 1 and let Fi≔Tr⁡(ρ​Ai)F_{i}\coloneqq\Tr(\rho A_{i}) and F⋆=maxi⁡FiF_{\star}=\max_{i}F_{i}. Given quantum copies of ρ\rho, there is a procedure which outputs an index i⋆i_{\star} such that Fi⋆≥F⋆−εF_{i_{\star}}\geq F_{\star}-\varepsilon with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, using

nAQTS=O⁡(με2​(log2⁡M+log⁡μδ)​log⁡μδ)n_{\mathrm{AQTS}}=O\left(\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon^{2}}\left(\log^{2}M+\log\frac{\mu}{\delta}\right)\log\frac{\mu}{\delta}\right) (176)

copies of ρ\rho, where μ≔log⁡1ε\mu\coloneqq\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}.

Proof.

This result is a simple extension of the quantum threshold search (QTS) algorithm of Ref. [6] where we run a binary search over the “threshold variable” θ\theta. We refer to Section III for a brief review of the quantum threshold search algorithm.

Define ξ=ε/12\xi=\varepsilon/12 and R=⌈log2⁡(12/ε)⌉+1R=\lceil\log_{2}(12/\varepsilon)\rceil+1. Let δ/R\delta/R be the tolerated failure probability of each call to the QTS algorithm.

We will initialize variables L=0L=0, U=1U=1 and i⋆=1i_{\star}=1 and update them after each step. At each step, L,U∈[0,1]L,U\in[0,1] are lower and upper bounds, respectively, on Fi⋆F_{i_{\star}} and F⋆F_{\star}.

At each step, we set θ=(L+U)/2\theta=(L+U)/2 and run QTS on A1,…,AMA_{1},\ldots,A_{M} with a common threshold θ\theta and accuracy ξ\xi. If QTS returns an index jj, then Fj>θ−ξF_{j}>\theta-\xi. If moreover θ−ξ>L\theta-\xi>L, we update

i⋆←j,L←θ−ξi_{\star}\leftarrow j,L\leftarrow\theta-\xi (177)

and otherwise leave i⋆i_{\star} and LL unchanged. If QTS returns “none”, we update

U←θ.U\leftarrow\theta. (178)

The size of the interval [L,U][L,U] shrinks as U−L↦U−L2+ξU-L\mapsto\frac{U-L}{2}+\xi. After RR steps, U−L≤2​ξ+2−R≤ε/3U-L\leq 2\xi+2^{-R}\leq\varepsilon/3, and in the event of no failures we have

Fi⋆≥L≥U−ε/3≥F⋆−ε/3,F_{i_{\star}}\geq L\geq U-\varepsilon/3\geq F_{\star}-\varepsilon/3, (179)

which is stronger than the required bound. From a union bound over the failure probabilities it follows that the total failure probability is at most δ\delta. The stated value for nAQTSn_{\mathrm{AQTS}} follows immediately from nQTSn_{\mathrm{QTS}} (c.f. Eq. (22)) and our choice of RR. ∎

Appendix D Details of numerics

In this section, we collect the details of the numerical plots in the main text. The general aim of the numerics shown in this paper is to establish that finding the closest Slater using our classical algorithm (classical) can still be a useful and meaningful task, at least for a small number of particles. Our algorithm also provides a new benchmark against which we can definitively assess the performance of heuristic closest Slater algorithms such as stochastic gradient ascent.

In Fig. 1c, we study the Fermi-Hubbard model [5]

H=−t∑⟨i​j⟩,σc†i​σcj​σ+U∑ini↑ni↓H\;=\;-t\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,\sigma}c^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}c_{j\sigma}\;+\;U\sum_{i}n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow} (180)

on a 4×44\times 4 square lattice with cylindrical boundary conditions (open along x^\hat{x}, periodic along y^\hat{y}) at a fixed electron filling n↑=n↓=2n_{\uparrow}=n_{\downarrow}=2 and we sweep over the coupling |U|/t∈[0,5]|U|/t\in[0,5] for both signs of UU. We produce the ground state by exact diagonalization. We compute and diagonalize the 1-RDM γ(i,σ),(i′,σ′)=⟨ci′​σ′†​ci​σ⟩\gamma_{(i,\sigma),(i^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime})}=\langle c^{\dagger}_{i^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}c_{i\sigma}\rangle to find the active orbitals with a fidelity tolerance ε=0.02\varepsilon=0.02. We parameterize the manifold of Slaters over the active space as follows. Writing n=n↑+n↓n=n_{\uparrow}+n_{\downarrow} and rr for the dimension of the active space, we fix an orthonormal frame as W0=(In0)∈ℂr×nW_{0}=\begin{pmatrix}I_{n}\\ 0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{C}^{r\times n}. Other nn-planes are specified by an (r−n)×n(r-n)\times n matrix ZZ, by setting Ω⁡(Z)=(0−Z†Z0)\Omega(Z)=\begin{pmatrix}0&-Z^{\dagger}\\ Z&0\end{pmatrix}, an antihermitian matrix, so exp⁡Ω⁡(Z)\exp\Omega(Z) is unitary, and then setting

W⁡(Z)=exp⁡[Ω⁡(Z)]​W0,W(Z)=\exp[\Omega(Z)]W_{0}, (181)

whose nn columns define another r×nr\times n orthonormal frame. We can restrict each entry of ZZ to [−π/2,π/2]⊕i[−π/2,π/2][-\pi/2,\pi/2]\oplus i[-\pi/2,\pi/2] and cover the entire manifold of Slaters [23]. This gives a compact parameterization with domain [−π/2,π/2]2​(r−n)×n[-\pi/2,\pi/2]^{2(r-n)\times n}, over which we form a covering net and perform an explicit search to evaluate 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT}.

In Fig. 4(a) we repeat this study with the same ground states represented by a neural quantum state (NQS), a multi-determinant Slater-Jastrow ansätz with four determinants and a neural Jastrow factor, optimized by variational Monte Carlo with stochastic reconfiguration [68]. From the trained NQS we run the search using only samples x∼|ψ⁡(x)|2x\sim|\psi(x)|^{2}. We estimate the 1-RDM, isolate the active space at tolerance ε=0.02\varepsilon=0.02 as above, and evaluate the fidelity of each trial Slater |S⟩|S\rangle with the estimator F^=|r¯|2/|r|2¯\widehat{F}=|\overline{r}|^{2}/\overline{|r|^{2}}, where r⁡(x)=⟨x|S⟩/ψ⁡(x)r(x)=\langle x|S\rangle/\psi(x) and the averages are taken over a fixed sample set. Dashed lines are the exact ED from Fig. 1c and the red band is the 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT} for the NQS, with width representing Monte-Carlo standard deviation over independent sample sets. This confirms the viability of computing 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT} using the closest Slater algorithm for modest system sizes using sample access to a neural quantum state representation. We note that the small upward drift at strong attractive coupling reflects the imperfect NQS approximation of the ground state.

In Fig. 4(b) we use 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT} as the ground truth against which to judge heuristic optimization. For Fermi–Hubbard ground states at fixed filling n↑=n↓=2n_{\uparrow}=n_{\downarrow}=2 and increasing system size mm, we run randomly initialized local gradient ascent on the Slater manifold and record the fraction of starts whose stationary fidelity reaches 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT} (within 5×10−35\times 10^{-3}). We fix U/t=2U/t=2 and compare ascent step budgets of 5050, 300300, and 20002000 iterations. For every budget the success rate falls sharply with mm (to a few percent or less by m=64m=64) and a larger budget shifts the curves upward without changing this trend. We note that a random Slater has fidelity of order one over the many body Hilbert space dimension with the target state, placing it on an exponentially flat region of the landscape where the gradient nearly vanishes and the ascent stalls. The search, by contrast, attains 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT} at every size. Therefore, randomly initialized local optimization may not be a reliable route to the closest Slater problem at scale, motivating our protocol.

In Fig. 4(c) we probe the optimization landscape of the closest Slater problem for several natural ensembles of pure and mixed states, confirming the F=2/3\mathrm{F}=2/3 threshold of Sec. V. We work in the nn-particle sector over m=2​nm=2n fermionic modes, whose occupation basis {|x⟩}\{|x\rangle\} of Slater determinants has dimension D=(mn)D=\binom{m}{n}. For a state ρ\rho the fidelity of a Slater is F⁡(S)=⟨S|ρ|S⟩\mathrm{F}(S)=\langle S|\rho|S\rangle, with 𝖮𝖯𝖳=max|S⟩⁡F⁡(S)\mathsf{OPT}=\max_{|S\rangle}\mathrm{F}(S), and a spurious stationary point is a stationary Slater with F⁡(S)<𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathrm{F}(S)<\mathsf{OPT}. For each state we compute 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT}, run many random-initialized local ascents to convergence, and collect the fidelities of the spurious stationary points they reach. Each state contributes a horizontal tick at 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT} and a point at every spurious level found. We sample four ensembles at n=5n=5, m=10m=10. In the Haar-random ensemble the state is pure with i.i.d. Gaussian coefficients ψx\psi_{x}. In the weakly correlated ensemble it is a determinant “cat”: a superposition of three to six Slater determinants at pairwise Hamming distance ≥2\geq 2 with comparable random weights. The random mixed ensemble is a rank-two mixture ρ=p⁡|v1⟩​⟨v1|+(1−p)|v2⟩​⟨v2|\rho=p|v_{1}\rangle\!\langle v_{1}|+(1-p)|v_{2}\rangle\!\langle v_{2}| of two independent Haar-random pure states, p∼U⁡[0.35,0.65]p\sim\mathrm{U}[0.35,0.65]. The physical ensemble consists of ground states of the spinless tt–VV chain

H=−t∑⟨i​i′⟩ci†ci′+V∑i=1mnini+1+∑i=1mεini,H=-t\sum_{\langle ii^{\prime}\rangle}\!c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{i^{\prime}}+V\sum_{i=1}^{m}n_{i}\,n_{i+1}+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\varepsilon_{i}\,n_{i}, (182)

spinless fermions on a periodic ring of m=10m=10 sites (cm+1≡c1c_{m+1}\equiv c_{1}, ni=ci†​cin_{i}=c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{i}) at half filling n=5n=5, with hopping t=1t=1, nearest-neighbor interaction VV, and on-site potentials εi\varepsilon_{i}. We refer to Fig. 9 for a plot of 𝖮𝖯𝖳\mathsf{OPT} in this model without disorder and with varying V/tV/t. For the figure in the main text, we draw V∼U⁡[−8,8]V\sim\mathrm{U}[-8,8] and, in 60%60\% of instances, weak disorder εi∼𝒩⁡(0,w2)\varepsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,w^{2}) with w∼U⁡[0.1,0.9]w\sim\mathrm{U}[0.1,0.9] (otherwise εi=0\varepsilon_{i}=0). A fifth, adversarial column contains states from the sharpness construction of Sec. V, whose planted spurious maximum sits at fidelity α2\alpha^{2} approaching 2/32/3; extending to n=16n=16 reaches a spurious fidelity of 0.6420.642. Across every ensemble all spurious stationary points lie strictly below 2/32/3, consistent with Theorem 5 and its mixed-state extension. For the natural ensembles they concentrate well below the threshold—at most ≈0.13\approx 0.13, 0.190.19, 0.390.39, and 0.490.49 for the mixed, Haar, weakly correlated, and physical ensembles respectively—so the bound is conservative there. Physical ground states rarely admit any spurious point; the physical column additionally includes verified charge-density-wave “cat” states which likewise remain below 2/32/3. Only the adversarial states approach the threshold, confirming that 2/32/3 is optimal in the worst case.
